priorities: Safety and production stability come first. We approve no launch without Pope's results on KPIs, suppliers and strain. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem. The 737 holds at 57 a month (684 a year) on the FAA-agreed gates, and hold is the only rate_737 value offered [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236, BG-0069].

Protect the rating. The column labels have changed this round: S2 is now an A350 Re-engine and S3 is the risk case (Airbus Delay Tactics, covert). The submitted plan's S3 may sit no more than $2B below Do Nothing's -0.83, so no lower than -2.83.
- Rows that pass: Do Nothing (-0.83); the Re-engine alone (-0.10); 10-year at Renton (-2.71, $0.12B clear); 10-year + Re-engine (-2.38); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine (-2.22).
- Rows that fail: 10-year at the new site alone (-2.87, short by $0.04B); every 7-year row (short by $0.85-1.36B); every via Embraer row (short by $3.61-4.08B) [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327, BX-0553].

One well-founded launch, not a bet. A launch needs an item value above +$1B in the expected column and no lower than -$1B in any plausible column. All three columns are plausible: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Delay Tactics are covert. Nothing clears this test this round.
- Best fps (10-year at Renton): -1.78 / -1.78 / -1.88 against hold.
- 787 Re-engine alone: +0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73. Even its best column is inside ε [BG-0021, BG-0022, BG-0066].

The next airplane only when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. Boeing is ready: net debt has been $0.0B since 2029, held in base and stress, and the 10-year rows are fundable. The engines are ready: the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine since 2036, and CFM is always available. The market gap has narrowed but is not closed. The 10-year at Renton has moved from about -4.3 (2035) to -1.78 against hold (2045). 2050 is the last round. Bring that case on the numbers, and give no date [BG-0068, B-2303, B-2315].

Keep the long-cycle position in view. Under Do Nothing, narrowbody preference falls from 34.0% (2045) to 27.7% (2050) and 16.0% (2060). Operating profit runs $0.5-1.4B a year below the status quo from 2048, while FCF stays at $12.66B or more. At our horizon we grant no extra downside for a long-term position, but we want that erosion beside every fps row [BG-0006, BG-0003, BX-0248].

frame.question:
Decision year 2045, round 3 of 4. NGSA has been in service since 2037, the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and the CFM ducted engine since 2041. Our own house is in order. Three questions:

1. Is the market there yet for the next airplane? The 10-year fps at Renton is now -1.78 against Do Nothing. That is the closest it has been. For the first time it passes Jay's buffer test (by $0.12B), and for the first time the objective premium it would need ($1.78-1.88B) fits under the $2B cap. Is that a case? Or is the gap closing mostly because the airplane is further away, not because the market came to us?
2. If we hold, what is waiting until 2050, the last round, worth? And what do we bring then?
3. The 787 Re-engine is worth +0.73 against hold at best. That is a tie at any odds. Hold it or bring it?

The test hasn't changed: "We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready" [BX-1296]. We decide on data, not dates, and Airbus's timeline doesn't set ours [B-2313].
frame.situation:
Decision year 2045, round 3 of dash-2050-cons.

WHERE WE STAND
- We have launched nothing and are on today's products.
- The 737 MAX holds at 57 a month: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate order offered.
- Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029 (2030 in stress) and holds to 2050 in base and stress.
- The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are done. My conditions for the next airplane (debt repaired, developments finished) are met [BX-1305, B-2326].

PUBLIC RECORD
- NGSA: in service since 2037, fitted with CFM + PW + RR. Airbus is on its A320 Alt plan.
- P&W and Rolls-Royce: both committed to the Joint Venture in 2035. GTF2 and UltraFan NB were folded into it, and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036.
- CFM: ducted engine ready since 2041. Its Embraer partnership has been live since 2042 (open and not exclusive).
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says the A350 "remains our widebody focus".
- Observed narrowbody delivery share: 33.1% in 2044 (684 against Airbus's 1,385).

DO NOTHING
- Scores -0.83 / -1.16 / -0.83. The labels have changed this round: S1 = rivals hold; S2 = Airbus launches an A350 Re-engine; S3 = risk case, Airbus Delay Tactics (covert). With no fps launched, Delay Tactics would be naked, so S3 equals S1.
- Narrowbody preference: 34.0% (2045), 27.7% (2050), 16.0% (2060).
- MAX deliveries: 684 (2045), 513 (2050), 346 (2055), 248 (2060).
- Waiting backlog: 432 (2045), 265 (2047), 0 by 2050.
- Operating profit runs $0.5-1.4B a year below the status quo from 2048. FCF stays at $12.66B or more and net debt at $0.0B. Value erodes; the balance sheet does not.

OBJECTIVES UNDER DO NOTHING
- Not met: the 50/50 split and incumbency (worst year 27.7%).
- Met: repairing the balance sheet and keeping it repaired, in base and stress.
- Engine enabler: dual or triple sources not met (the MAX flies CFM only); three narrowbody makers met. No fps launched in 2045 or later is in production by 2050, so no order this round can meet the dual-source line for 2050.

THE GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1 / S2 / S3)
- 787 Re-engine alone: +0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73. Best plan in S1 and S3.
- 10-year at Renton: -1.78 / -1.78 / -1.88. At the new site: -1.94 / -1.94 / -2.04.
- 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -1.29 / -2.83 / -1.39. The best fps row in S1 and S3.
- 7-year: -2.70 to -4.48. It trails the 10-year by $1.21-1.53B in every column.
- Via Embraer: -5.51 to -7.23. It trails the Solo 10-year by $4.03-4.23B.
- Renton adds +0.16 to +0.17 on a 10-year fps and +0.22 to +0.23 on a 7-year. It adds nothing while the fps holds.
- On top of a 10-year fps, the Re-engine adds +0.49 / -1.05 / +0.49.

TREND OF THE 10-YEAR AT RENTON AGAINST DO NOTHING
- 2030: -4.39 to -5.26 (-5.26 in the column that came true, NGSA on the Alt plan).
- 2035: -4.24 to -4.35.
- 2045: -1.78 to -1.88.
- Ten years of discounting at 10.5% multiplies by 0.37. That alone would take 2035's -4.29 to -1.58. So most of the narrowing is the discount clock, not the market turning (inference; Jay to check).

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes, on the brief. Pope's seat to confirm.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
   - Boeing: yes. Net debt is $0.0B, and every 10-year row holds it in stress.
   - Technology: yes. Codes 5, 6 and 7 give CFM plus the Joint Venture.
   - Market: no. Every fps row trails Do Nothing by more than ε in every column.
   - Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
3. What if certification takes longer than we think? S3 is Jay's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83. Three fps rows now pass:
   - 10-year at Renton, by $0.12B;
   - 10-year + Re-engine, by $0.45B;
   - 10-year at Renton + Re-engine, by $0.61B.
   So on those rows the fps call is mine, not his veto.
4. Is this doing less, better? Do Nothing beats every fps row by more than ε in every column. The Re-engine is within ε of Do Nothing at any odds [BX-1239].

BOARD RISKS (guidance, not red lines)
The Board says it would veto:
- launch_10yr at any site, in any combination. It fails Business case (needs more than +$1B), Downside (below -$1B in every column) and the market leg. At the new site alone it also fails Rating first (S3 -2.87).
- launch_7yr: S3 is $0.85-1.36B short of the limit, and stress net debt is not held ($0.5-4.7B).
- launch_via_embraer.
- re787: launch in any combination. Its best column (+0.73) is below +$1B. Paired with a 10-year fps it breaks the Downside limit (-1.05 to -1.06 in S2).
- A launch carried by a premium. Its tests read the grid.

It would approve:
- every hold;
- Renton, with Pope's wind-down result;
- a 10-year Solo in a round whose grid supports it.

It wants in the package:
- the Do Nothing erosion to 2060;
- the value of waiting until 2050;
- the trend since 2030;
- Jay's buffer and Fundable results, with numbers;
- Pope's results;
- my standing rulings on H1, H3, H4 and H5;
- every premium logged, with any hold its own tests require shown apart;
- no fps date.

frame.asks_cfo:
Jay, you're my independent check on estimates [BX-1316]. Run the slip leg as the baseline [BX-0553]. Numbers, please. Note that the labels have changed: S2 is now an A350 Re-engine, and S3 is the risk case your test reads.

1. BUFFER TEST, ROW BY ROW (S3 against -2.83). My reading:
- Pass: Do Nothing (-0.83); the Re-engine alone (-0.10); 10-year at Renton (-2.71, by $0.12B); 10-year + Re-engine (-2.38, by $0.45B); 10-year at Renton + Re-engine (-2.22, by $0.61B).
- Fail: 10-year at the new site (-2.87, by $0.04B); every 7-year row (by $0.85-1.36B); every via Embraer row (by $3.61-4.08B).
Confirm or correct, and name the rows you would veto. Is a $0.12B pass robust when the board doesn't price doctrine's +3-year slip for a clean sheet?

2. "FUNDABLE WHEN THE 777X TURNS" [BX-0547]. My reading:
- Pass: every 10-year row, the Re-engine alone and Do Nothing ($0.0B stress).
- Fail: the 7-year rows ($0.5-4.7B) and via Embraer ($3.8-10.1B).

3. CASH TIMING for a 2045 launch on the brief's standard curve:
- 10-year fps: $60.32B over 2045-55, peak year about 2051.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2045-50.
Set these against base and stress FCF. Base FCF itself erodes under Do Nothing: $13.27B in 2050, $12.76B in 2055. How much falls on surplus the Board reserves [BX-0556]? Quote the undiscounted penalties ($19.1B / $22.0B / $52.5B / $0.6B) for scale only.

4. THE VALUE OF WAITING UNTIL 2050, the last round. This is the question I most need answered. Check my inference:
- The 10-year at Renton went from -4.39 to -5.26 (2030), to -4.29 (2035), to -1.78 (2045) against Do Nothing.
- Ten years of discounting alone (x0.37) would give -1.58. So the narrowing is mostly the discount clock, not the market turning.
- If that's right, a 2050 grid shows about -1.1 (x0.61) for an EIS of 2060 and a 27/73 long-run split: still below Do Nothing, and about $2B short of the Board's bar.
Then tell me:
(a) Does the board's 20-year window from EIS, together with the replacement demand that rises after 2060 (544 in 2060, 1,244 in 2065), change that?
(b) Is there any path on this board by which an fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε in 2050?
(c) What does waiting cost that the grid doesn't price?

5. SLIP. The full cost, once, of doctrine's +3-year fps slip: 2055 becomes 2058, and the long-run split moves from 32/68 to 29/71.

6. 787 RE-ENGINE.
- Your odds of an A350 Re-engine this round. You had 40% in 2035, and Airbus has now held twice.

cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.83 in S3, so the limit is -2.83. Three fps rows pass: the 10-year at Renton (-2.71, by $0.12B), the 10-year with the Re-engine (-2.38) and the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine (-2.22). Nine fail, and under the team rule I veto them: every 7-year row ($0.85-1.36B short), every via Embraer row ($3.61-4.08B) and the 10-year at the new site alone ($0.04B).

A pass is not a case. Your inference holds, and more: the discount clock explains all of the narrowing. Net of the clock, the gain has lost about $0.2B since 2035. In 2045 dollars the 10-year at Renton trails Do Nothing by $11.9B, against $10.5B in 2035 dollars. Doctrine's three-year slip costs $1.4-2.0B, all in, once; $0.12B absorbs two or three months of it. On the board, waiting to 2050 costs nothing. I project -1.1 to -1.3, still $2.1-2.3B short of the Board's bar. The later window and the 2060s replacement wave slow the slide but don't turn it. What waiting costs is off the board: workforce, suppliers, a 737 base at 16% by 2060.

The Re-engine is a tie. At my 35% odds it's worth +0.19, near zero after a 2050 haircut, and Do Nothing has the higher worst column. Hold it; I log $0.19B.

Hold everything, barring an A350 Re-engine on the record. The balance sheet stays fully restored.

ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes; the KPI, strain and supplier gates are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery [BX-1331]. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and hold is the only rate order, so my KPI veto has nothing to act on. 57 a month holds. LEAP-1B stays a watch item, and an easing one: CFM delivered about 2,239 narrowbody engines in 2044 against 2,593 in 2035, while our call is unchanged at 1,368.

Second, engineering capacity. Strain confirmed: a 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B) with no slack, since a 1-year Re-engine slip breaches H4. It overlaps a 7-year by 5 years ($3.0B), which is barred, and any 2050 fps by zero. The unpriced item is people. By 2050 we will have run no major development for 23 years. Any launch needs a funded hiring and transfer plan first [B-1941, B-0729].

And finally, disciplined profitable growth [BX-1327]. Operations backs the 10-year ramp at Renton, $1.21-1.53B ahead of the 7-year. I sign the Renton wind-down, conditionally: it follows the ramp, never leads it. At a 32/68 split our whole narrowbody demand is about 41-56 a month, so a new site buys capacity the market won't fill. Embraer trails Solo by $4.03-4.23B and adds nothing we lack [BX-1330]. Code 7 gives two mature sources.

But no fps beats Do Nothing; the best trails by $1.29B. I recommend hold on every lever.

decision.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and you'll get the same straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane isn't there yet. On paper it looks closer than it was. I've looked hard at why, and I'm not going to tell you something has turned when it hasn't. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it. In the meantime we're keeping our engineering teams and our suppliers ready, because readiness doesn't keep by itself.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We'll keep giving customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: DO NOTHING IN EVERY FIELD
- Orders: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody call: the three work streams [BX-1296], debt first read on the grid [BX-1305], Airbus's timing does not set ours [B-2313], and doing less [BX-1239].
- On the 787 Re-engine, my record breaks the tie: doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. The odds of an A350 Re-engine are Malave's (Low), and the Board's Business case test points the same way.
- Every cell below was checked against the brief in work/r3_ceo_decide_calc.py.

1. TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding veto covers nine rows: every 7-year row, every via Embraer row, and the 10-year at the new site alone (S3 -2.87, short by $0.04B). I accept it and have no override.
- Three 10-year rows pass his buffer test, so the fps call on those is mine.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on: no Rate Increase is offered and no problem is live.
- Her H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is moot because I don't order it.
- No red line is breached, and both memos recommend these orders.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. Nothing is live, and LEAP-1B is a watch item that is easing (Pope).
(2) Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready?
- Boeing: yes. Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029, and the 10-year rows are fundable.
- Technology: yes. CFM and the Joint Venture are both mature by any EIS from 2052.
- Market: no. Every fps row trails Do Nothing by more than ε in every column.
- Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I read S3 as Malave's slip leg, with a limit of -2.83. His results are in section 4.
(4) Is this doing less, better? Yes. Nothing beats Do Nothing by more than ε in my expected column [BX-1239].

3. TESTED CASE (S1 / S2 / S3)
- Submitted, Do Nothing: -0.83 / -1.16 / -0.83. Expected -0.95 at 35% odds of an A350 Re-engine.
- Rejected rows, shown against Do Nothing:
  - Re-engine alone: -0.10 / -1.97 / -0.10 (+0.73 / -0.81 / +0.73); expected -0.75.
  - 10-year at Renton: -2.61 / -2.94 / -2.71 (-1.78 / -1.78 / -1.88).
  - 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -2.12 / -3.99 / -2.22 (-1.29 / -2.83 / -1.39).
  - 7-year at Renton: -3.82 / -4.15 / -3.97 (-2.99 / -2.99 / -3.14).

final.public_statement:
I've said for a long time that we'll do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and you'll get the same straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable. The 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 have been flying with customers for years. The balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is ready too: there are good, mature engines out there from more than one maker. The market case for our next airplane isn't there yet. On paper it looks closer than it was. I've looked hard at why, and I'm not going to tell you something has turned when it hasn't. So we're not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours.

When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners, and we won't take a fixed-price bet on it. In the meantime we're keeping our engineering teams and our suppliers ready, because readiness doesn't keep by itself.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. We'll keep giving customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep investing in Charleston.

We'd rather do fewer things and do them well. The financials will follow our production performance.

5. fps: HOLD, EVEN THOUGH THE BUFFER PASSES AND A PREMIUM WOULD FIT
- The market leg fails, and so does my debt-first test: the best fps trails Do Nothing by $1.29B (S1) and the 10-year at Renton by $1.78B.
- My frame said most of the narrowing was the discount clock. Jay says it is all the clock, and I take his number.
  - Net of the clock, the market moved $0.20B against us.
  - In decision-year dollars the gap went -$7.8B (2030), -$10.5B (2035), -$11.9B (2045).
  - The case is getting worse, not better. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" doesn't even apply here [BX-1300].

  - The 50/50 split is the company's mission, not a reason to launch an airplane the grid says loses value.

- Ramp and form for the record: the 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.21-1.53B in every column. Via Embraer trails Solo by $4.03-4.23B and adds no IP we lack (Pope).

6. THE VALUE OF WAITING, SAID PLAINLY
- On the board, waiting costs nothing. Jay projects the 2050 10-year at -1.08 to -1.28 against Do Nothing, $2.1-2.3B short of the Board's bar, and he finds no 2050 path that clears ε.

- I won't launch to avoid saying it: "It is so much more important that we do this right than fast" [BX-1241].
- Waiting does cost things the grid doesn't price: workforce, supplier health, a 737 base falling to 16% by 2060, and MAX volume down 64%. I answer those with the non-public moves: a risk-reduction team, a hiring plan and funded suppliers.

7. 787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD

- The Board vetoes it on Business case.
- Pope's workforce-bridge point is real but unpriced. It bridges to a 2050 fps that Jay finds no case for, and a warm risk-reduction team does that job for less.
- I accept that this likely closes the option: 2050 is worth about +0.44 at best.

8. STANDING RULINGS
- H1: stays lifted. The condition was met, not waived.
- H2: cannot bind.
- H3: first half lifted. Second half open: no A350 Re-engine is on the record.
- H4: a 2045 Re-engine with a 2045 10-year overlaps 2 years, legal with no slack. With a 7-year it overlaps 5 years and is barred.
- H5: never cancel a launched programme.
- H6: not engaged.
- H7: no trigger on this board.

- Under-disclosure: no fps date.
- Cash for readiness: suppliers kept funded.
- Inward focus.
- Certification optimism: no trigger, since nothing is in certification.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
On the A350 Re-engine, any one of these would change my result:
- A grid that shows the Re-engine at least $1B over hold and not negative in any plausible column.

In 2050 I would apply the same test to a 2050 launch, with rule 3 checked at submission. My pre-read is +0.61, below $1B.
cfo.memo:
Round 3 (2045), brief's grid. Recommended: ngsa hold, engine code none (fixed in service; I defer to Lars), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board item.

Peak cash. NGSA spend ended in 2036 ($35.52B / 7 over 2030-36). The Alt plan's $0.75B ran at $0.094B a year to 2044. A350 Re-engine: $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year in 2045-49, with zero overlap and zero strain. Peak $1.0B against $5.2B leaves $4.2B of headroom for all prepayments combined. Pass.

Net cash at end-2049, before any new buyback (an inference, round-2 method): 48% payout $80.5B, or $75.5B with the Re-engine; 30% $123.7B / $118.7B; 50% $75.7B / $70.7B. The Re-engine takes 6% of 2045-49 FCF. A new buyback sized to the yearly surplus (about $6.5B at 48%, after the Re-engine) fits the 10% authority. No equity raise.

Robustness. Both rows stay positive in their worst column: default S4 +13.29, Re-engine S7 +13.33. The item is +0.89 in S1-S5 and -0.50 / -0.51 in S6 / S7: inside the -$2B line, +0.75 weighted. It turns negative in two plausible columns and never reaches $1B, so it fails the company's added-move test: a binding soft veto. At a best margin of +0.89, no override can carry it. For the record, the failure is on value, not cash.

Waiting: a 2050 launch is worth about +0.61, also below $1B; rule 3 closes it if the 787 is re-engined.

Deleted: all Delay Tactics (naked $48.32B fine, rules 4-5).

ops.would_change_mind_if:
- **An A350 engine on the public record that is mature by the Re-engine's EIS.** For example, Rolls-Royce launches an UltraFan widebody or an A350 Trent upgrade. An UltraFan widebody launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, so it fits a 2050 Re-engine launch (EIS 2055) with four years of margin. My engine test would then pass.
- **A non-default engine.** If CFM/GE offered its GEnx upgrade (mature since 2033) for the A350 with a certification path inside the five-year development, it would still need the team's $1B under Step 3.
- **An EIS re-timed to the engine.** If the ExCo moved the EIS to the engine's year, on the record and as a window, readiness would pass. The item would fall to about +0.82 (2051) or +0.56 (2056); this is my pure-discount inference. The $1B launch condition is then for Faury and Toepfer to apply.
- **The operating case if the engine were secured.** I would see no operating reason to hold: zero overlap, NGSA at its last step, and A320 lines closing and freeing staff. This round the engine decides, not the $1B rule.
- **Events that move me the other way.** A reported supply crunch, quality escape or safety event (on the NGSA ramp or the A320 tail) would fail more tests and freeze new concurrency. A 787 Re-engine on the record closes the Re-engine under rule 3.
- **Delay Tactics.** Only an fps on the record would reopen them, and then at most one `poaching` move while a programme of ours is in development. The Board's veto still binds.
ops.memo:
My tests come from my role, not my record. Confidence: Very low.

Both changes running this round pass. NGSA's last step is small: 1,306 to 1,339 a year, then 1,366. That needs 2,612-2,732 engines a year, below the 2,770 we carried in 2044 with no crunch. The A320 tail is 28 aircraft in 2045 and none from 2047. Build them on the fewest lines, keep certified staff to the last aircraft, and release the surplus A320neo engine slots. Safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch pass on both rows.

The A350 Re-engine passes engineering capacity: NGSA development ended in 2037, so there is no overlap and no strain. It passes absorption too. The A350 line has delivered its planned 70 a year since 2026, with no event reported.

It fails readiness on the engine. No widebody engine for the A350 has been launched. UltraFan widebody is ready six years after launch: 2051 at the earliest, and 2056 on Rolls-Royce's own sequence. The GEnx upgrade is a 787 engine that has never flown on the A350. Doctrine wanted the engine committed a year before our launch; it has not been. Engine supply reset our 2027 rate. I will not launch an airframe into an engine gap.

On the five pillars this is a re-timing note. On my readiness test it is a binding soft veto, and at +0.89 no override can carry it.

Hold. Delay Tactics are deleted (rule 4, integrity). Secure the engine, then test again in 2050.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in service, and its ramp-up is completing in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and we will keep running it on that clock. This is how we prepared the Airbus of the 2030s, and it is how we will serve our customers into the next decade. To the end of the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: the all-default package. ngsa hold, engine code fixed (none), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board item.

ORDER OF ARGUMENT
1. Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081]. Two transitions run this round: NGSA's last ramp step (1,306, then 1,339, then 1,366) and the closure of the last A320 lines (28 in 2045, none from 2047). Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch on both rows, and no event is reported. One condition applies: no engine enters service before it is mature. No widebody engine for the A350 is on the record as mature for a 2050 EIS, so a Re-engine EIS would have to move rather than take an immature engine. On the pillars that is a re-timing note, not a breach (Wagner).
2. Ramp. It stays disciplined and controlled to the last step [AX-0010]. Nothing new goes on top of the closure that Lars cannot pass.
3. Prepare the next decade on its technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006]. I would welcome a late, cheap A350 derivative [AX-0082, A-0090], but not ahead of its engine.
4. What I can take to the Board. Nothing beyond the default, on this round's tests.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE AND PILLAR BREACHES
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Rule 5: nothing is in development.
  - Integrity applies to bottleneck and both.
  - Every row breaks the -$2B line: one move -11.46 / +0.06 / +0.06 / +0.44 / +0.06 / -11.46 / +0.05; both moves -11.72 / -0.13 / -0.13 / +0.22 / -0.13 / -11.72 / -0.14.

final.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in service, and its ramp-up is completing in a disciplined and controlled way. It flies on robust, multi-source engine supply from CFM and from the Pratt & Whitney-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. We brought it into service on the clock of maturity, and we will keep running it on that clock. This is how we prepared the Airbus of the 2030s, and it is how we will serve our customers into the next decade. To the end of the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we keep the in-service fleet fully supported. We are securing the engines, structures and materials our own production needs. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. We continue to fund our programmes from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? It's the same game: the installed base, not share for its own sake. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages."

This round the board leaves us one real choice, and it isn't a hard one. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting. The only levers left are an Open Fan and lobbying on emissions, and the airframer has already set that date. The NGSA has flown since 2037. An Open Fan launched today is ready in 2055. One launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, after the board's narrowbody window closes in 2056. So no Open Fan reaches an airframer in this game. Both Open Fan rows lose more than their bill in both columns.

So the question isn't what to launch. It's three things.
1. Is the fleet flying today safe and durable on field data? That covers the LEAP fleet and the new single-aisle engine counting since 2041. Any flag ranks ahead of everything else on this page.
2. Do we keep delivering through the NGSA ramp and the longer A320 tail, with time-on-wing kits and shop-visit material ahead of OE rate?
3. Are we candid about what we got wrong? The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035. Last round I called it "more likely than not" to stay off the record, and I was wrong. Today's hold row is -28.04, against -25.03 forecast and -27.00 booked. We tie that out in numbers. In private, we say plainly that both objectives will be reported as not met.

How we win: hold every field, run the business, keep RISE whole as technology with Safran, and keep CFM on offer to every airframer. Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order, decide any tie.

  - Allowance: the cost is $17.48B with Lobby and $20.01B alone. Both are above the $15B allowance, and above the allowance plus the round cap.
  - It buys no objective, because it can't be ready by 2050.
  I won't stretch the allowance.

- Lobby does nothing without an Open Fan.

Safran gate:
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We are not asking Safran to fund a product no airframer can take, and there is no reason on the record why it would.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE, and it is not proposed without an Open Fan.

- genx: GE alone.

Candour, kept in private:

- Both objectives will be reported as not met: NB share is 47.2% in 2050, and the Open Fan can't be ready by 2050. No PV is given up for either.

What would change the lean: nothing on the grid. A safety or durability flag from Mohamed wouldn't change the holds, but it would go to the Board at once and go to the top of our statement. "We don't want to be rash, but we need to get after this straight away."

- My condition was a volume, not a share, and I hold to it. It stays out of expected_pv_b, and the volumes-first condition stands.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (ask 10)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores
tests.numbers:
Worst column for hold: S1 at -28.04, which is also my expected column. It is 0.02 below the weighted -28.02 on .75 / .25, and 0.09 below S2. Not in either column (rough figures, inference):
(a) A Boeing fps on a 7-year clock with a code that drops CFM, for example code 4. It would take MAX slots we hold as sole source from 2052: about -2.4. On a 10-year clock or via Embraer: about -0.25, because only 2055-56 fall inside the window.
(b) A widebody re-engine or Trent 1000 upgrade that undoes the GEnx step (about 9 WB engines a year, 2048-61): about -0.4. UltraFan WB on a re-engine would be more.
(c) A change to the Joint Venture: no rule path undoes a formed one, so low.
(d) My usual three. On airframer delivery slowdowns, our NB engines for 2045-56 are worth $29.7B of PV, so 5% fewer deliveries is about -1.5 and 10% about -3.0. Tariff escalation and a global recession are not in the grid.
(e) Durability: the brief has no time-on-wing or inspection data. Any reserve is booked in the round the need is found, not in this grid.
(f) The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, and a 2050 round remains.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence
tests.threshold: For each launch: bill year, ready year, first year of share gain, inside the NB horizon to 2056 (inference: my dated sequences applied to the board)
tests.numbers:
Hold launches nothing.
The sequence delivered on programmes already running, on the observed data:
- Ducted: bill 2035, ready 2041, first gain 2041 (13.5% to 23.2% on the NGSA). Gross about 6.07 against its $6B bill; payback about 2056, back-loaded as I said in 2035.
- Embraer: counts from 2042 (26.9%).
- GEnx: counts from 2042 (WB 42.0% to 44.8%).
For the record, an Open Fan's sequence fails: bill 2045, ready 2055 (Ali's date), no share gain inside the NB horizon, and losses from 2045.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan with two or more projects (the $2B strain); each item passes only net of the strain it adds
tests.numbers:
- Hold runs no project in development. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx are all ready, and the row's -2.00 of strain is the 2035 Ducted's, sunk.
- An Open Fan alone would be one project with no new strain; the rows tie without it. Lobby is not a development project.
- The GE9X is not live.

tests.name: Terms (ask 8)
tests.threshold: No launch-era pricing, no price concession, and no CFM narrowbody price talk without Safran, in any public statement or other move
tests.numbers:
Culp's draft line carries no price, concession, launch-era terms, volume or rate.
- 'Airbus asked for long-term supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran': the answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity going to Safran first and nothing in public.
- 'On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better': GE alone, won on product, with no price in public.
- 'CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer' is an offer of supply, not of terms.
- Advice: any LEAP kit or shop-visit offer stays at standard terms, with no free upgrade. I'll re-check the final text at the veto check.

tests.name: Guide low (ask 9; advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed (inference: my guidance habit)
tests.numbers: Book expected_pv_b at -30.15: the S1 hold row (-28.04) less Embraer's in-row value of about $2.11B on my model, until a volume is agreed. On round 2's grid figure (+1.97) it would be -30.01. No S2 upside (+0.09) is booked. I raise it to -28.04 when an Embraer volume is agreed. Last round I booked -27.00 and came in $1.04B high, so the guide stays at the low end.

vetoes.plan: Conditional: open_fan: launch, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground:
capex: it fails pays-for-itself, volumes-first and the premium cap. My veto right is an inference from my price/cost and volumes-first record; under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.
- The Open Fan alone is -20.01 / -19.97 against hold, $12.01B / $11.97B beyond its $8B bill.
- Open Fan + Lobby is -17.48 / -17.45, $8.48B / $8.45B beyond a $9B bill on my strain reading.
- Its cost against the best non-RISE plan is $20.01B or $17.48B. That is above the $15B RISE allowance, and above the allowance plus the $2.0B round cap ($17.0B).
- No airframer path in either column: the NGSA has been in service since 2037, and the Open Fan would be ready in 2055.
This is not a cancel: RISE stays whole as technology (hard rule 5).

vetoes.plan: Conditional: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan launched or live
vetoes.ground: capex: it fails pays-for-itself. The veto right is an inference that binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. Lobby alone is about -1.00 in both columns (inference: a $1B bill, no row on the grid, and no board effect without an Open Fan). With an Open Fan, it falls with the vetoed Open Fan.

vetoes.plan: Conditional: any real Embraer spend (integration or support), or any Embraer number, committed before an Embraer volume is agreed
vetoes.ground: capex: it fails volumes-first. The veto right is an inference from 'we need to work the exact volume assumptions' applied as a capital test; it binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. No Embraer airframe or volume is on the record, and none is proposed. This is a standing condition, not triggered by Culp's lean.

vetoes.plan: Standing: any public statement or other move (the Airbus long-term supply answer, the GEnx-787 answer, any LEAP kit or shop-visit offer) that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or talks CFM narrowbody price, rate or capacity without Safran
vetoes.ground: terms. The veto right is an inference from my pricing record and the joint-decision rule; it binds under the team rule, and on a statement alone the Board reads it as a recommendation. Culp's draft line and other moves pass as written: no price, no concession, the Airbus answer joint with Safran first, and the GEnx offer GE alone with no public price.

vetoes.plan: Advice: expected_pv_b, column weights and the strain reading in the record
vetoes.ground:
Not a veto (advice only).
- Book -30.15, not -28.04: Embraer's +2.11 stays out until a volume is agreed.
- Run the weights at .75 / .25, not .60 / .40: Boeing has no commitment on the record.
- Correct the Open Fan + Lobby bill to $9B. The rows tie with no new strain (inference). The Board's $11B leaves every call unchanged.
- Book any durability reserve in the round the need is found.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Six things would move me.
(1) An Embraer volume is agreed: I raise the guide by about $2.1B, to -28.04.
(2) A Boeing fps reaches the record with its clock and code: I re-weight. A 7-year clock with a code that drops CFM is about -2.4 (rough), outside both columns.
(3) An Ali durability or safety flag on field data: the holds don't change, but I book the reserve in the round we find it and the agenda changes.
(4) The 2050 grid shows a lever beating hold with its bill charged: I test it then. No Open Fan can, because a 2050 launch is ready in 2060.
(5) Safran declines the joint Airbus answer, or wants terms in public: I re-run the terms test.
(6) The GM's strain rule differs from my reading: I re-state the bills. No call turns on it.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the money ties out.

Your item values match to the cent: Open Fan -20.01 / -19.97; with Lobby -17.48 / -17.45; Lobby on top +2.53 / +2.52. On strain, the rows carry none: my rough model ties both Open Fan rows to the cent without it and is $2B off with it. So the bills are $8B and $9B, not the Board's $11B (inference). Either way each loses more than its bill, costs above $17.0B, and no airframer can take it inside the window. Hold is best in both columns. Premium $0, game total $0 of $4.0B, RISE allowance unused.

Reconciliation. The Joint Venture is the whole -3.01. On the observed shares we ran about 13% on the NGSA before our engines counted, against the 18% round 2 priced: five points lower at every step. That's -3.15, less +0.14 because Embraer is worth more on a lower base. Against my book, -1.04 is that -3.15 plus Embraer's +2.11 I left out. Your share calls were right on the column; the column was wrong. I listed the Joint Venture and never priced it. We've been proven wrong on that one before.

But the good news is the programmes delivered: the Ducted took us from 13.5% to 23.2% in 2041, Embraer to 27% in 2042.

Floor: no new R&D, payout whole, no rating risk. Weights: I'd run .75 / .25; nothing turns on it.

Book -30.15: S1 less Embraer until a volume is agreed.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my date veto): every ready year in the orders and options
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted at launch + 6; Open Fan at launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts at launch + 7; GEnx at launch + 3, counting from 2042 with no re-engine on the record. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. Inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times.
tests.numbers:
Culp's ask (6), recomputed from rules.md and the brief.
- Ducted (hold, on the record): 2035 + 6 = 2041, ready since 2041.
- Embraer (hold): 2035 + 7 = 2042, counting since 2042.
- GEnx (hold): 2030 + 3 = 2033. It counts from 2042, with no re-engine on the record. WB share 44.8% since 2042.
- Open Fan, options B and C: max(2045 + 10, 2045) = 2055. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060.

Grid (S1 / S2):
- hold: -28.04 / -27.95;
- Open Fan: -48.05 / -47.92;
- Open Fan + Lobby: -45.52 / -45.40.
Items against hold, which I recomputed to the cent:
- Open Fan: -20.01 / -19.97;
- Open Fan + Lobby: -17.48 / -17.45;
- Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 / +2.52.
Both Open Fan rows carry the wait penalty, so they are valued on 2055, not on an earlier year. Hold adds no date.

The 'ready by 2050' objective cannot be met, because 2045 + 10 = 2055. Any premium or claim resting on it would rest on a year five years earlier than the board allows, and it would fail. Culp's frame claims none.

What test stands behind 2041? None on ducted hardware in my evidence. It is the board's development time, and it is now a date on the public record. I report no slip, because I have no evidence of one. I certify no gate result, because I have none.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my date veto): Culp's draft public line and other moves (Culp's ask 9)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back. No Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, no ready year before launch plus development years, and no RISE ground-test, flight-test or entry year (hard rule 6).
tests.numbers:
Line by line:
- 'Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order': no date.
- 'the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers': no year. I can stand behind it on the record. The Ducted has been ready since 2041 (public table), and CFM is fitted on the NGSA, in service since 2037. The board counts the Ducted's share on NGSA deliveries from 2041. That it is flying is my reading of those two facts (inference): the record says 'ready', not 'in service'. Add nothing to it: no cycles, no time on wing, no 'durable', no year. We have no field numbers.
- 'We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and what we don't know yet': a commitment with no date. Today we have delivery data and nothing on durability.
- 'kits stay ahead of OE rate through the ramp': no date.
- The Airbus answer 'jointly with Safran': no rate, no year.
- 'RISE stays a technology programme ... the airframers will set its date': no ground-test, flight-test or entry year. My 2022 fly demo, 'by the middle of this decade', became 'this decade'. Promise none.
- No 'next generation', no Ducted figure, no rival named.

Other moves F(i) to (vii) carry no public dates. 2055, 2060 and 2056, and the objective note, stay in the rationale and with the Board.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice; Culp's ask 6)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service avoids the 35 pp wait penalty (20 pp with Lobby). Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
The first new narrowbody is the NGSA, in service since 2037.
- Launch in 2045: ready 2055, 18 years after the NGSA. In S2 a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055, the same year, but the NGSA came first, so the penalty applies in both columns.
- Launch in 2050: ready 2060, 23 years after the NGSA and 4 years after the board's narrowbody window closes in 2056.

Grid: Open Fan alone -20.01 / -19.97; with Lobby -17.48 / -17.45.

Confirmed: no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game. The 2055 date itself is correct, so this is not my veto. Hard rule 2 bars the launch.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted and Embraer (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new narrowbody is in service, so lateness does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: ready 2041, 4 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry. It has earned its +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041.
- Embraer: counts from 2042, 5 years after the NGSA.
- In S2 a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055. The Ducted is ready 14 years ahead of it and Embraer counts 13 years ahead, if Boeing keeps code 7.
Hold carries both. There is nothing to launch.

tests.name: Physics (wording check)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Without a fuel-burn claim this is a wording check on the statement (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Neither the brief nor the draft line makes a fuel-burn claim.
- 'Next generation' does not appear. 'Our new single-aisle engine' is not a next-generation claim.
- Culp's H3 holds: the Ducted gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain. It is a defence, never the next generation.
- Culp's 20% line binds RISE. No RISE product is proposed, so the line is not engaged.

RISE facts for the Board: designed for 'more than 20%', ready for sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen-capable. In tests with Airbus, open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's.

tests.name: Durability first: no plan trades durability for fuel burn or schedule
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers:
The test applies because Culp's frame puts durability first.
- Hold everything trades nothing: no new programme, no fuel-burn target, no schedule to compress.
- The plan keeps kits and shop-visit material ahead of OE rate.
- The Open Fan options would start a new hot-section development on the constrained suppliers while the installed fleet's durability data is still open. See the supply-load test.

tests.name: The Ducted's hot-and-harsh gate and enhanced inspection, on field data (Culp's asks 2 and 3; the Board's first ask)
tests.threshold:
- Harsh time on wing against the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 cycles, not the LEAP's about 4,800. The company target is 8,000 harsh and 17,000 neutral.
- The gate passed on turn-on, turn-off testing before entry into service.
- Enhanced-inspection findings on safety-critical parts, in new make and MRO, from the first engine.
Field or test data only.
tests.numbers:
Not applicable because the test cannot be run. This is not a pass.
- The brief's only field data is deliveries. It has no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle, inspection, supplier-level or kit data, and the frame says the same. My own evidence ends in November 2025, before any ducted hardware existed.
- The engine has been in service four years (2041-2045). The fleet leader's cycles against 7,000-8,000 are not in the data.
- Did the gate pass before 2041? There is no evidence either way. The record shows ready in 2041 on the board's development time. No slip was reported, and no pass is certified.
- Enhanced inspection is institutionalised in new-make shops and MRO (my 2024 words). Findings from the first Ducted engine: none in the data.

Is missing data a flag? No. A flag is a finding: a failure turned on in test, or found in the field or in inspection. I have none, and I will not raise one on analysis. But missing data is not a clean bill either. It goes to the Board as an open item, and the cross-functional team owes the numbers. Until they exist, nothing in public or in private may claim the Ducted meets the yardstick.

tests.name: Installed LEAP fleet: the LEAP-1B kit (Culp's ask 4)
tests.threshold: A durability fix counts only when it is certified and the failure is turned off in test. A kit that does not turn the harsh-environment failure off is an installed-fleet flag, ahead of any new programme.

tests.name: LEAP supply review on field data, and the tripwire (Culp's ask 5; the Board's ask)
tests.numbers:
Pass on the delivery leg only.
- Every year from 2035 to 2044, CFM NB engines equal 2 x aircraft delivered x our share, to within 2 engines of share rounding: 2,592 engines on 1,704 aircraft (2035); 2,604 on 1,714 (2036, the peak); 2,144 on 1,570 (2040); 2,283 on 1,804 (2041); 2,237 on 2,069 (2044).
- No aircraft on the record waited on a CFM engine. Airbus went from 886 to 1,385 aircraft (2040-44) on the Alt plan, and Boeing held 684.
- Load: 2044 ran 367 engines below the 2036 peak of 2,604. On hold, volume is 2,106 in 2045 and 1,749 in 2050.
- The 9 suppliers at 15 sites: there is no supplier-level data. They are not certified, and I will not certify them on analysis.
- Kits and shop-visit material against OE rate: there is no kit data, so I cannot say this leg is met on field data.

Tripwire: not tripped on the OE leg, and the kit leg cannot be read. It was written to sequence Ducted development hardware behind the fleet. That development ended in 2041, so it has nothing left to sequence. The fleet-first rule stands through the A320 Alt-plan tail (CFM has 60% of A320neo engines) and the NGSA ramp, and any rationing call is cross-functional.

Supply in my record is only Culp's description of my job. No evidence: following doctrine.

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine; Culp's ask 8)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. Inference: my supply role is in Culp's words only (the board's strain rule).
tests.numbers:
Hold adds no project and no strain. R&D stays at -4.00 (the 2035 Ducted) and strain at -2.00, both already in the row.

Open Fan + Lobby: the board's rule counts Lobby as a project, so the pair is two projects and carries the $2B strain. That is the board's count, for Ghai to verify. On the shop floor I correct it:
- Lobby loads no supplier; the Open Fan is the one hardware project.
- But the Open Fan would put a new compact core and fan on the same constrained hot-section suppliers that carry LEAP kits, shop-visit material and the Ducted's production through the NGSA ramp.
So the stack is real, and the grid does not pay for it: -17.48 / -17.45 with Lobby, -20.01 / -19.97 alone. I recommend against.

No evidence: following doctrine (the board's strain rule).

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into the in-service engines while RISE matures (inference).
tests.numbers:
- GEnx: hold is the only option. The upgrade is on a proven architecture, ready since 2033 and counting since 2042 at 44.8% WB. Taking it to 787 customers puts the same proven engine on more aircraft. It is not a new engine.
- Narrowbody: RISE technology keeps flowing into the in-service LEAP and the Ducted while RISE matures. Hot-section cycles are the moat.

tests.name: Safety call (Culp's ask 1)
tests.threshold: Any problem or order that touches safety or durability goes to a cross-functional team, never to one person. Any flag goes to the Board at once.
tests.numbers:
No safety or durability flag is open on the evidence: the gate and LEAP-1B tests found no data and no finding. All orders are holds.

The frame sends any rationing call and the safety report (other move vi) to a cross-functional team. Any flag goes to the Board at once and to the top of the agenda and the statement. That meets the test. A flag, if one comes, arrives with the cross-functional answer on evidence.

tests.name: RISE test record (Culp's ask 7)
tests.threshold: RISE test progress reported, and no open durability failure, before any Open Fan launch. No RISE date in public.

vetoes.ground:
Dates not backed by real testing, binding grounds 1 and 2: 'if it's not turn on and turn off, I will not believe the outcomes'; 'it's not on the back of a theory. It's not on the back of analysis.'

Inference note: my words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern whether to believe durability-fix results. That they give me a veto over programme dates is an inference. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with test evidence.

Every value on the grid rests on the board's development times (2041, 2042, 2055), so nothing is vetoed now. I will re-check the final orders and the statement at the veto check.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in 2045, alone or with lobby_emissions: launch
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a date veto: 2055 is the correct ready year.
- It is 18 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry into service, so the wait penalty applies in both columns. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, after the 2056 window closes. No airframer path exists in this game.
- It would stack a new hot section on the constrained suppliers that carry the installed fleet.
- RISE results after October 2025 are not in my evidence, so no test backs a product.
Hard rule 2 bars it. Keep RISE whole as technology. We failed twice. We got it done.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions: launch without an Open Fan
vetoes.ground: Advice. There is no date issue, because Lobby takes effect at once, but it does nothing on its own. No evidence: following Culp and doctrine. Technical facts, if ever needed: RISE is designed to be ready for sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen-capable, and open-fan noise came in below the LEAP's in tests with Airbus.

vetoes.plan: Wording in the public statement
vetoes.ground:
Advice.
- Keep 'now flying with our customers' and add nothing to it. No cycles, no time on wing, no 'durable' or 'mature' for the new engine or the LEAP-1B: we have no field numbers.
- No 2055, 2060 or 2056. The objective note stays private.
- Never 'next generation' for the Ducted.
- 'We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field' commits us to report when the numbers exist. Do not fill it with analysis.

vetoes.plan: Open evidence items for the Board (not a flag)

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test or field data would change my mind, never analysis.
(1) A flag. A Ducted or LEAP finding in the field or in inspection would be one: a harsh-environment failure turned on that the design does not turn off, a finding on a safety-critical part, or a fleet leader removed short of the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 harsh cycles. I raise it at once, with the cross-functional answer. The holds stay; the agenda and the statement change.
(2) The LEAP-1B kit. A certification result showing the kit does not turn the harsh-environment failure off is an installed-fleet flag, ahead of everything.
(3) Supply. Field data showing kits or shop-visit material behind OE rate, OE deliveries below airframer rate, or a supplier site not cleared. Then kits come first, and the rationing call goes to a cross-functional team.
(4) The Open Fan. Nothing on this board moves it. I would need an airframer whose first new narrowbody enters service no earlier than the Open Fan's ready year, plus RISE ground-test, flight-test and compact-core durability results turned on and turned off. With the NGSA flying since 2037, that cannot happen in this game.
(5) A Boeing fps on the record. It changes the column, not my dates: a 7-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2052, and a 10-year one in 2055. The Ducted is ready for either.
ops.memo:
In 2035 I told this Board that a failed gate moves the date, not the gate, and that you would get field numbers in 2045. Here is what I have.

Dates. Ducted: 2035 plus 6, 2041. Embraer and the GEnx count from 2042. An Open Fan launched today is ready in 2055, eighteen years after the NGSA entered service. Launched in 2050, it is ready in 2060, past the 2056 window. No Open Fan reaches an airframe in this game. No option is valued on an earlier year. My date test passes. No veto.

Deliveries. From 2035 to 2044 every aircraft got two engines at our share: 2,237 engines on 2,069 aircraft in 2044. No aircraft waited on us.

Durability. The brief has no time on wing, no harsh cycles, no inspection findings and no kit data. The yardstick stays the CFM56 in harsh service, 7,000 to 8,000 cycles, not 4,800. I cannot tell you the Ducted meets it. I cannot tell you it misses it. The LEAP-1B kit's outcome is not in my evidence. The 9 suppliers are not certified.

Missing data is not a flag: a flag is a failure turned on. It is not a pass either. I sign off nothing on results. The cross-functional team owes you the numbers.

Public line: "now flying" stands on the record. Add nothing to it. No cycles, no "durable", no year, no "next generation".

Hold everything. Kits ahead of OE rate. RISE whole. Embraer, lobbying: No evidence: following Culp.

other_moves.move: RISE continues whole as a 50-50 technology programme with Safran
other_moves.detail: Funded as technology and not cancelled for cost (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0398]. We launch no product. In public there is no ground-test, flight-test or entry year (H6, Ali's date test) [CX-0009]. The airframers set the date for the architecture [CX-0205]. We bring RISE test results from after October 2025 to the Board once they are on the record. No product claim is made, so my 20% line is not engaged [CX-0217].

other_moves.move: CFM keeps answering Airbus's long-term supply request (A320neo tail and NGSA), jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: Made as CFM, jointly with Safran. Price, rate and capacity go to the partner first, on standard terms [CX-0184]. Nothing goes out in public: no price, concession, volume, rate or delivery year. Ghai's volumes-first condition stands: the NGSA volume assumptions are worked with Airbus inside this answer before any number goes out [CX-0944]. The board does not price this move.

other_moves.move: CFM engines stay on offer to every airframer
other_moves.detail: CFM offers its engines on any new single-aisle Boeing launches, and the Embraer partnership stays open and not exclusive. No airframer is locked out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. There are no price, terms or dates in public, and any pricing goes to Safran first.

other_moves.move: GEnx upgrade brought to 787 customers with Boeing (GE alone)
other_moves.detail: This answers Boeing's public request. The upgrade is GE's own programme, ready since 2033 and counting since 2042 (WB share 44.8%). It is won on product, not price [CX-0599, CX-0615]. There is no Safran gate and no price in public. It is not a 787 Re-engine order, and the board does not price it.

other_moves.move: LEAP fleet first: kits and shop-visit material ahead of the OE delivery rate

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate through the ramp, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus asked for long-term engine supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold everything (Do Nothing) on every field. Every order is at default, so there is no Board item. The hold row is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and -27.95 in S2. Premium $0. No overrides.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It's the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting. The only live levers are open_fan and lobby_emissions, and the airframer has already set that date: the NGSA has been in service since 2037. We win this round by running the fleet, keeping RISE whole, keeping CFM on offer to every airframer, and being straight about what we got wrong and what we don't know.

GRID (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7)
- Hold: -28.04 / -27.95.
- Open Fan: -48.05 / -47.92.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -45.52 / -45.40.
- Items against hold (Ghai and Ali both verified to the cent):
  - Open Fan alone: -20.01 / -19.97;
  - Open Fan + Lobby: -17.48 / -17.45;
  - Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 / +2.52;
  - Lobby alone: about -1.00 (inference; no row).
- Weighted at .75 / .25: hold -28.02; Open Fan -20.00; Open Fan + Lobby -17.47. No call turns on the weights.

MY TESTS
1. No birthright [CX-0564]: neither column has a rival taking our slot. In S2, Boeing selects all three makers. The cases that could take a slot (a 7-year fps with a code that drops CFM) sit outside both columns, so they go on the watch list.
2. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]: no launch beats hold.
   - A new narrowbody is on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect: -20.01 alone and -17.48 with Lobby.
   - Each loses more than its bill: $12.01B beyond $8B; $8.48B beyond $9B on Ghai's strain reading.
   - Nothing makes that risk worth taking.
3. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1. Boeing said it is not launching this year and gave no date.
4. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]:
   - An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, 18 years after the NGSA's entry. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056.
   - So no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game. I'm saying that plainly rather than stretch the test.
   - The RISE allowance cannot cover $17.48B or $20.01B. Both are above $15B, and above $15B plus the $2.0B round cap.
   - I know my installed-base lens could dress this up as 'seeding the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. It doesn't apply when no airframer can take the engine inside the window.
5. Ducted as a defence (H3): it is ready, it has earned +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041, and there is nothing to decide.
6. Can the suppliers carry it: holding adds no project and no strain. The open supplier items are below.
7. Next generation: no fuel-burn claim and no 'next generation' wording. The 20% line binds RISE and is not engaged.
8. Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads the next row by $17.48B, far outside the $1B ε.
9. Premium cap: $0, with the game total at $0 of $4.0B.

EXCO, UNDER THE TEAM RULE
I proposed hold, and both colleagues recommend hold.
- Ghai's binding vetoes are all conditional and none is triggered:
  - an Open Fan, alone or with Lobby;
  - Lobby alone;
  - Embraer spend before a volume is agreed;
  - price or terms talk without Safran.
  His terms test passes my statement as drafted.
- Ali's date veto is conditional and not triggered: every value rests on the board's development times, and the statement carries no date. He raises no safety or durability flag.
- So I have no failed test to answer, and the overrides field is empty.

STRAIN READING (correction to the Board's inference)
Ghai's model ties both Open Fan rows to the cent with no new strain. Ali confirms that Lobby loads no supplier. So the bills are $8B (Open Fan alone) and $9B (Open Fan + Lobby), not $11B. This is inference, and no call turns on it.

SAFRAN GATE (H7) [CX-0184, CX-0166]
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We ask Safran to fund no product that no airframer can take inside the window, and holding asks nothing of the partner.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan, so nothing goes to Safran.
- ducted (hold): ready, a defence of the installed base both partners share. No new order.
- partner_embraer (hold): no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer (volume, terms, spend) goes to Safran first.
- The Airbus long-term supply answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

RECONCILIATION (candid, in numbers)
- Round 2's S1 forecast was -25.03. I booked -27.00 (Embraer's +1.97 left out), and today's row is -28.04.
- R&D (-4.00) and strain (-2.00) came in as forecast, so the whole -3.01 is engine value.
- On Ghai's derivation from the observed shares (inference: the bulletin doesn't state the folding rule):
  - The Joint Venture's rule effect is CFM -10 pp on the NGSA. Against the solo engines we priced, the GTF2's -5 gave way but the UltraFan's -10 effectively stayed, so CFM ran 5 pp lower on the NGSA at every step.
  - That 5 pp is worth -3.15. Embraer is worth +0.14 more on the lower base. Net -3.01, nothing left over: the Joint Venture is all of the gap.
  - Against the book, the -1.04 is -3.15 plus Embraer's +2.11, which is in the row but was not booked.
- My 2045 and 2050 share calls ran about 3 pp high (5 pp times the NGSA's 65-72% of NB deliveries). The arithmetic was right on the column; the column was wrong.
- I called a Joint Venture commitment 'more likely than not' to stay off the record. Both partners had public conditional commitments and the airframe test was met. I listed it and didn't price it. That one's on me. From now on, a rival's standing public commitment is a live column.
- The programmes delivered: the Ducted took CFM from 13.5% to 23.2% on the NGSA in 2041 on schedule, and Embraer took it to about 27% in 2042.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T (field data)
- What we know: deliveries. In every year from 2035 to 2044 each aircraft got two engines at our share (2,237 engines on 2,069 aircraft in 2044), and no aircraft waited on a CFM engine.
- What we don't know: in 2035 we told the Board it would get field numbers in 2045, and we don't have them. The brief carries no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle, inspection, supplier-level or kit data. Ali certifies no gate result and raises no flag on analysis.
- I take this as an open item, not a pass. The cross-functional team owes the five items listed in other moves, and any failure comes to the Board at once. None of this changes a hold; it sets the agenda.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record doesn't address Embraer handling, Lobby or the game's Open Fan window, so company doctrine (profile section 6; dashboard_game section 2) drove those calls. Money follows Ghai's tests. Dates and readiness follow Ali's.

NEXT ROUND (2050)
No lever on this board lifts NB share. An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, past the window. I expect to hold again unless a Boeing fps, a Re-engine or a field finding changes the facts.

final.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Our first job is the fleet flying today: the LEAP fleet and our new single-aisle engine, now flying with our customers. We'll tell you what we're seeing in the field, and we'll tell you what we don't know yet. Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of the OE delivery rate through the ramp, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn.

Airbus asked for long-term engine supply, and we're working that through with them, jointly with Safran. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it, one engine at a time.

On the 787, we'll keep making the GEnx better for Boeing's customers.

RISE stays a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set its date.

No new programme this round. We're running the business we've got, and running it well. It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
final.rationale:
DECISION: hold everything (Do Nothing) on every field. Every order is at default, so there is no Board item. The hold row is the best plan in both columns: -28.04 in S1 and -27.95 in S2. Premium $0. No overrides.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It's the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. The Ducted, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all ready and counting. The only live levers are open_fan and lobby_emissions, and the airframer has already set that date: the NGSA has been in service since 2037. We win this round by running the fleet, keeping RISE whole, keeping CFM on offer to every airframer, and being straight about what we got wrong and what we don't know.

GRID (S1 rivals hold / S2 Boeing 10-year fps, code 7)
- Hold: -28.04 / -27.95.
- Open Fan: -48.05 / -47.92.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -45.52 / -45.40.
- Items against hold (Ghai and Ali both verified to the cent):
  - Open Fan alone: -20.01 / -19.97;
  - Open Fan + Lobby: -17.48 / -17.45;
  - Lobby on top of the Open Fan: +2.53 / +2.52;
  - Lobby alone: about -1.00 (inference; no row).
- Weighted at .75 / .25: hold -28.02; Open Fan -20.00; Open Fan + Lobby -17.47. No call turns on the weights.

MY TESTS
1. No birthright [CX-0564]: neither column has a rival taking our slot. In S2, Boeing selects all three makers. The cases that could take a slot (a 7-year fps with a code that drops CFM) sit outside both columns, so they go on the watch list.
2. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609]: no launch beats hold.
   - A new narrowbody is on the record, so S1 shows the launch's own effect: -20.01 alone and -17.48 with Lobby.
   - Each loses more than its bill: $12.01B beyond $8B; $8.48B beyond $9B on Ghai's strain reading.
   - Nothing makes that risk worth taking.
3. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1. Boeing said it is not launching this year and gave no date.
4. The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]:
   - An Open Fan launched in 2045 is ready in 2055, 18 years after the NGSA's entry. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the narrowbody window closes in 2056.
   - So no Open Fan reaches an airframer path in this game. I'm saying that plainly rather than stretch the test.
   - The RISE allowance cannot cover $17.48B or $20.01B. Both are above $15B, and above $15B plus the $2.0B round cap.
   - I know my installed-base lens could dress this up as 'seeding the next 30 years' [CX-0555]. It doesn't apply when no airframer can take the engine inside the window.
5. Ducted as a defence (H3): it is ready, it has earned +10 pp on the NGSA since 2041, and there is nothing to decide.
6. Can the suppliers carry it: holding adds no project and no strain. The open supplier items are below.
7. Next generation: no fuel-burn claim and no 'next generation' wording. The 20% line binds RISE and is not engaged.
8. Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads the next row by $17.48B, far outside the $1B ε.
9. Premium cap: $0, with the game total at $0 of $4.0B.

EXCO, UNDER THE TEAM RULE
I proposed hold, and both colleagues recommend hold.
- Ghai's binding vetoes are all conditional and none is triggered:
  - an Open Fan, alone or with Lobby;
  - Lobby alone;
  - Embraer spend before a volume is agreed;
  - price or terms talk without Safran.
  His terms test passes my statement as drafted.
- Ali's date veto is conditional and not triggered: every value rests on the board's development times, and the statement carries no date. He raises no safety or durability flag.
- So I have no failed test to answer, and the overrides field is empty.

STRAIN READING (correction to the Board's inference)
Ghai's model ties both Open Fan rows to the cent with no new strain. Ali confirms that Lobby loads no supplier. So the bills are $8B (Open Fan alone) and $9B (Open Fan + Lobby), not $11B. This is inference, and no call turns on it.

SAFRAN GATE (H7) [CX-0184, CX-0166]
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We ask Safran to fund no product that no airframer can take inside the window, and holding asks nothing of the partner.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan, so nothing goes to Safran.
- ducted (hold): ready, a defence of the installed base both partners share. No new order.
- partner_embraer (hold): no new order. Anything that goes to Embraer (volume, terms, spend) goes to Safran first.
- The Airbus long-term supply answer stays joint, with price, rate and capacity to Safran first.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

RECONCILIATION (candid, in numbers)
- Round 2's S1 forecast was -25.03. I booked -27.00 (Embraer's +1.97 left out), and today's row is -28.04.
- R&D (-4.00) and strain (-2.00) came in as forecast, so the whole -3.01 is engine value.
- On Ghai's derivation from the observed shares (inference: the bulletin doesn't state the folding rule):
  - The Joint Venture's rule effect is CFM -10 pp on the NGSA. Against the solo engines we priced, the GTF2's -5 gave way but the UltraFan's -10 effectively stayed, so CFM ran 5 pp lower on the NGSA at every step.
  - That 5 pp is worth -3.15. Embraer is worth +0.14 more on the lower base. Net -3.01, nothing left over: the Joint Venture is all of the gap.
  - Against the book, the -1.04 is -3.15 plus Embraer's +2.11, which is in the row but was not booked.
- My 2045 and 2050 share calls ran about 3 pp high (5 pp times the NGSA's 65-72% of NB deliveries). The arithmetic was right on the column; the column was wrong.
- I called a Joint Venture commitment 'more likely than not' to stay off the record. Both partners had public conditional commitments and the airframe test was met. I listed it and didn't price it. That one's on me. From now on, a rival's standing public commitment is a live column.
- The programmes delivered: the Ducted took CFM from 13.5% to 23.2% on the NGSA in 2041 on schedule, and Embraer took it to about 27% in 2042.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T (field data)
- What we know: deliveries. In every year from 2035 to 2044 each aircraft got two engines at our share (2,237 engines on 2,069 aircraft in 2044), and no aircraft waited on a CFM engine.
- What we don't know: in 2035 we told the Board it would get field numbers in 2045, and we don't have them. The brief carries no time-on-wing, harsh-cycle, inspection, supplier-level or kit data. Ali certifies no gate result and raises no flag on analysis.
- I take this as an open item, not a pass. The cross-functional team owes the five items listed in other moves, and any failure comes to the Board at once. None of this changes a hold; it sets the agenda.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
My record doesn't address Embraer handling, Lobby or the game's Open Fan window, so company doctrine (profile section 6; dashboard_game section 2) drove those calls. Money follows Ghai's tests. Dates and readiness follow Ali's.

NEXT ROUND (2050)
No lever on this board lifts NB share. An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, past the window. I expect to hold again unless a Boeing fps, a Re-engine or a field finding changes the facts.
