ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. These are the only values the brief lists (round3.md §3). The grid has one row: -1.65 in S1 and -1.68 in S2.

WHY `gtf2_solo: hold`. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture when it formed in 2035. It is no longer a separate programme: its engine is the Joint Venture engine, ready since 2036. Hold keeps that in-service engine and its durability work whole.

WHY `jv_with_rr: hold`. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a commitment can be withdrawn only before formation (rules.md). Hold keeps it on the published terms: one engine, the gear and core P&W's work-share and IP [P-1233], and partner content only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.

ANSWERS TO CALIO

(1) Proposal: as above. Holding both fields costs us nothing technically.

(2) Readiness: confirmed.
- The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2. GTF2 launched in 2030 and was ready in 2036 (launch + 6). Formation + 6 would have been 2041 and UltraFan NB 2037, so ready = 2036.
- NGSA entered service in 2037 on code 7, with CFM + PW + RR fitted. The one-year margin held, and the code cannot change now.
- S2, an fps 10-yr launched in 2045, enters service in 2055: a 19-year margin. An fps 7-yr would enter service in 2052 (16 years), and an fps via Embraer in 2055. A 2050 launch would enter service in 2057 or 2060.
- No second development is running: no new programme on the record, and $0 of new R&D. Programme R&D is $2.00B in total, booked in 2035 (brief §1).
- Caution (bias check on my own reassurance): the board sets ready at launch + 6 and models no slip. That the 2036 date held on the record is the rule's outcome, not evidence that our dates no longer slip. The company's +1.5 to 2 year derivative-entry prior is not refuted by it.
- Condition on the fps offer: we offer the engine as certified. Any fps-specific rating, installation or derivative change is an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence, not a promise.

(3) In-service durability: the bad number first.
- The brief and our files hold no time-on-wing, LLP life against plan, shop-visit findings, removal causes or hot-and-sandy data for the Joint Venture engine. That is eight years into service, 2037-45.
- They also do not hold the 2036 gate data (endurance hours, LLP life at EIS, maturity-gate status) that the Board asked for in round 2.
- I invent none. That is what we report to Governance and Public Policy.
- Process for the report (doctrine and my record):
  - Report by operating environment, never as a fleet average. In 2023, three quarters of the GTF fleet flew in cool climates and that hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122].
  - Track fleet leaders in hot-and-sandy operation separately.
  - Report LLP life by part family against the life declared at EIS [PX-0128].
  - Report shop-visit findings by cause.
- On the public record, Airbus took the engine into service in 2037 on its 'clock of maturity' ('no engine will enter service before it is mature'). That is Airbus's word, not our data.

(4) Parts and capacity: ground 2 PASS.
- Load (brief §1):
  - 730 engines in 2040, 1,024 in 2044 (the peak; +40%, about the size of the 2023 castings step [PX-0125]; the 2043-44 step alone was +13%).
  - Then 976 in 2045 (-4.7%) and 928 to 987 a year to 2056.
  - The highest year after the peak is 987 (2051), 3.6% below it. The largest yearly step after it is +2.8% (2049).
  - Round 2 projected +53% to 1,068. The squeeze came in smaller.
- Installed base on the brief's counts: 7,339 engines delivered in 2026-36 and 13,937 P&W NB engines in 2026-44 are coming into the shops. The board does not model shop visits, so I give no shop-visit peak date or interval. '2044-47' is the OE plateau, not a dated shop-visit peak.
- As the A320neo OE tail ends under the Alt plan, GTF OE demand on pacing parts falls away and those parts go to MRO.
- Ranking on the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123], decided daily and reviewed by the ExCo weekly [PX-0131]:
  1. AOG spares.
  2. MRO material for engines in the shop. Shops wait on parts, not capacity [PX-0124].
  3. GTF Advantage kit parts, fitted to engines already in the shop.
  4. OE installs: NGSA long-term-agreement slots and the A320neo tail.
- This can leave Airbus short of engines on some days. That trade is Calio's to balance with Airbus [PX-0099][PX-0110], and the tie-break says the fleet beats a new engine.
- Supplier quality gates come before each rate step, including the small post-2048 steps, because the powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040].
- The brief shows no live P&W quality escape or supply problem, and no order launches anything.

(5) Configuration control.
- On the record, nothing has changed: the engine is the one ready since 2036, with no new programme and $0 of new R&D.
- The published rule stands:
  - Partner content enters only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence.
  - We instrument any new feature in our own application rather than take a partner's design at face value [PX-0168][P-1215].
  - P&W signs durability only on what it tested.
  - The gear and core stay P&W's work-share and IP [P-1233].
- The engineering-change log itself is not in my brief. It goes to the committee with the durability report.

(6) Product answer to CFM's ducted engine: YES, as an internal other move, on four conditions.
- (a) Time on wing ahead of fuel burn [P-1360]. No new programme, no derivative, no board R&D.
- (b) Each change goes in as an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence.
- (c) Kit parts rank behind AOG and shop material.
- (d) The same in-service engineering team that works the shop findings does the work.
On those conditions it is fleet work, not a second engine: it cuts shop visits and therefore pacing-part demand. It changes no payoff, and it is not a price answer.

(7) GTF Advantage kit.
- It continues at standard terms with pass-through pricing [PX-0117] (pass-through for the kit is inference).
- My last fleet-configuration figure is 60% in June 2023, with a target of 90% within 2-3 years [PX-0116]. The evidence has no outcome for that target and no 2045 figure, so we publish none.

(8) Two-ground ruling on hold/hold: both pass. No veto.

ROUND-2 BOARD RECOMMENDATIONS IN MY LANE
- Withdraw test (rec 1): overtaken. My technical trigger was not hit. Formation came in 2035, two years before EIS. It folded GTF2 in as the one engine, with no second development and no change to the configuration being certified.
- Durability gate (rec 3): the gate data are not in my brief (see 3). The +1.5 to 2 year prior is the company's, not mine.
- Fleet first (rec 7): adopted as above. The brief shows no escape through the +40% step, but the board models no quality, so that is not proof that there was none.

STATEMENT CHECK (Calio's draft): PASS. 'Ready since 2036' and 'flown on NGSA since 2037' are facts on the bulletin. 'Claim the durability the fleet data show' is right, and the draft gives no forward date and no share projection.
Advice, not binding: 'more time on wing from every engine ... our new engine ... alike, and that work is not done' reads as a known shortfall on the Joint Venture engine. We have no data either way. Keep the known GTF shortfall, and for the new engine say we will report what the fleet data show, bad news first.

Lesson carried: three quarters of the GTF fleet flew cool in 2023, which hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall, so we report no fleet averages.

tests.name: Pacing parts and capacity (veto ground 2)
tests.threshold: If the brief or bulletin shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, fleet lift comes first and an unconditional launch fails. If none is shown, report pass and note that the board does not model parts (inference)
tests.numbers:
No launch is ordered, and the brief and bulletin show no live P&W quality escape or supply problem.
- Load (brief section 1): 730 engines (2040) rising to 1,024 (2044 peak; +40%; +13% from 2043 to 2044). Then 976 (2045), 968 (2046), 976 (2047), and 928 to 987 a year to 2056.
- The highest year after the peak is 987 (2051), 3.6% below it. The largest step after it is +2.8% (2049).
- Installed base: 7,339 engines delivered 2026-36 and 13,937 delivered 2026-44 are coming into the shops. The board does not model shop visits, so I give no dated shop-visit peak.
- The A320neo OE tail is ending on the Alt plan.
- Ranking on the roughly 30 pacing parts, decided daily and reviewed weekly: AOG spares, then shop material, then Advantage kit parts, then OE.
- Supplier quality gates come before each rate step.

tests.name: Contain first
tests.threshold: If a quality escape is in the brief: contain it and give a dated recovery before any new commitment (inference)
tests.numbers: The round 3 brief and bulletin show no quality escape. Because the board models no quality, that is not proof that there was none.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: Advice only, as this board has no strain charge: one new development at a time. A folded GTF2 and the formed Joint Venture count as one programme (inference)
tests.numbers: No development is running. The one engine has been in service since 2037. New R&D is $0, and programme R&D is $2.00B in total (booked in 2035, brief section 1). Incremental time-on-wing work is sustaining engineering by the team that works the shop findings. Look-ahead: any 2050 engine item would be ready in 2056 or later, a second development during the shop-visit tail. It is not needed for readiness, because the in-service engine meets any fps EIS.

tests.name: Architecture and Joint Venture configuration control
tests.threshold: The engine extends the GTF (inference from PX-0129). The gear and core stay P&W's work-share and IP [P-1233]. Partner content enters only after EIS as an engineering change with its own test evidence and is instrumented in our application. P&W signs durability only on what it tested (inference)
tests.numbers: The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2 (it inherited GTF2's schedule), so it is our architecture. The published 2035 terms stand. The record shows no change: no new programme, $0 R&D, and readiness unchanged since 2036. The engineering-change log is not in my brief and goes to the committee with the durability report.

tests.name: Other move: incremental durability and time-on-wing work inside existing R&D (CEO other-move test 2)
tests.threshold: Go only if it pulls no engineers or pacing parts from the fleet, puts time on wing ahead of fuel burn, adds no new programme or board R&D, and puts each change in with its own severe-environment test evidence (inference)
tests.numbers: It passes on those four conditions. Kit parts rank third, behind AOG spares and shop material, and the same in-service engineering team does the work. It cuts shop visits and therefore pacing-part demand. It has no payoff on the board, and it is not a price answer to CFM.

tests.name: Cancel and withdraw check
tests.threshold: When cancel or withdraw is legal, propose hold and report readiness. Otherwise not applicable (doctrine; my record is silent on cancels)
tests.numbers: Neither is legal. GTF2 folded in 2035, and withdrawal is possible only before formation (rules.md). The round-2 withdraw test is overtaken. My technical trigger (touching the in-service GTF2's gear, core or configuration, or starting a second development during the ramp) was not hit: formation came in 2035, before the 2037 EIS, as one engine.

tests.name: Single aisle
tests.threshold: No widebody engine [PX-0127]
tests.numbers: Both orders are narrowbody. P&W has no widebody move on this board.

vetoes.plan: Orders `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (my proposal)
vetoes.ground: None invoked. Ground 1 passes: no order puts an engine on an airframe, the engine was ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS, and hold compresses nothing. Ground 2 passes: no launch, and no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem in the brief.

vetoes.plan: Draft public statement
vetoes.ground: Not binding now; the draft passes. Ground 1 would bind at the veto check if the statement claimed proven durability, time-on-wing or LLP figures not in the fleet data, or promised an fps-specific rating or configuration before it is tested. Advice: don't imply a known shortfall on the Joint Venture engine, because we have no data either way.

vetoes.plan: Other moves (fleet first, Advantage kit, incremental durability, Joint Venture engine offered to an fps)
vetoes.ground: Not binding now. Ground 2 reopens if any move ranks OE installs, kits or fps work ahead of AOG spares on the pacing parts, or steps rate without supplier quality gates. Ground 1 reopens if partner content or an improvement enters the certified configuration without its own test evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any concession, discount or free upgrade to win the fps code
vetoes.ground: Not my ground, so not binding. I agree with value, not share: standard terms and pass-through pricing (inference).

ops.would_change_mind_if:
(1) In-service data show a durability shortfall on the Joint Venture engine: hot-and-sandy time on wing below plan, LLP life short of plan, or an unplanned shop-visit finding. It then goes first in the statement and the committee report. The incremental work refocuses on that fix, and the fps offer carries the fixed configuration only once it has its own test evidence.
(2) A brief shows a live quality escape, rising AOG or a supply break. I contain first, give a dated recovery, and OE gives way to the fleet.
(3) The incremental durability work starts pulling engineers or pacing parts from the shops. We drop it.
(4) Partner content enters the certified configuration without its own test evidence, or rights over the gear or core pass. I invoke ground 1 and flag the red line.
(5) In 2050, a new engine item appears on the sheet. It must serve a committed airframe and be ready by its EIS. The in-service engine already meets any fps EIS, so I would ask what a second development buys during the shop-visit tail.
ops.memo:
The bad number first. Our Joint Venture engine has flown on NGSA for eight years, and I can't put one time-on-wing, LLP-life or shop-visit figure in front of the Governance and Public Policy Committee. They're not in my brief, the board doesn't model them, and I won't make them up. A caution on us: the 2036 ready date held because the board sets ready at launch plus six. That's a rule, not proof our dates stopped slipping.

What I can confirm. The engine is the folded GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036, in service 2037. One engine, no second development, $0 of new R&D. It meets any fps EIS: 2052 on a 7-year, 2055 on a 10-year. Gear and core stay ours; partner content goes in only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.

Parts. OE peaked at 1,024 engines in 2044, up 40% from 730 in 2040, then 976 in 2045 and 928 to 987 a year to 2056. No step above the peak. About 13,900 P&W engines delivered since 2026 are coming through the shops as the A320neo tail ends. On the 30 pacing parts: AOG first, shop material second, kits third, OE last, daily. No live escape in the brief. Ground 2 passes.

I propose hold and hold, the only legal values. No veto. Durability work inside existing R&D: yes, as fleet work that cuts shop visits.

My record is one event, June 2023. The Joint Venture, configuration and in-service views are seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
other_moves.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit to the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing [PX-0088][PX-0106]. There is no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100]. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration. We publish no 2045 share figure, because we do not have one: Eddy's last figure is 60% in June 2023, with a 90% target [PX-0116], and the evidence has no outcome for that target. We give no dated AOG recovery, because my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0098][PX-0104]. Kit parts rank third on the pacing parts, behind AOG spares and shop material. The move changes no payoff on the board.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on pacing parts through the OE plateau and the shop-visit tail
other_moves.detail: On the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123] the ranking is: (1) AOG spares; (2) MRO material for engines in the shop, since shops wait on parts, not capacity [PX-0124]; (3) GTF Advantage kit parts for engines already in the shop; (4) OE installs, meaning NGSA long-term-agreement slots and the A320neo tail. Allocation is decided daily and reviewed by the ExCo weekly [PX-0131]. Supplier quality gates come before every rate step, including the small steps after 2048, because the powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040]. The load is 1,024 NB engines at the 2044 peak, 976 in 2045, and 928 to 987 a year to 2056. About 13,900 P&W NB engines delivered in 2026-44 are coming into the shops. Eddy's correction stands: 2044-47 is the OE plateau, not a dated shop-visit peak, because the board does not model shop visits. Some days this leaves Airbus short of engines. I balance that with Airbus jointly [PX-0099][PX-0110], and the fleet comes first [PX-0080].

other_moves.move: In-service durability report on the Joint Venture engine to the Governance and Public Policy Committee, bad number first
other_moves.detail: Eddy reports. The bad number first: after eight years in service (2037-45), we have no time-on-wing, LLP-life, removal or shop-visit figures for the Joint Venture engine, and no 2036 gate data, in front of the committee. We invent none. Going forward the report gives: time on wing by operating environment, never as a fleet average, with hot-and-sandy fleet leaders tracked separately [PX-0122]; LLP life by part family against the life declared at EIS [PX-0128]; shop-visit findings by cause; and the engineering-change log, confirming that no partner content entered the certified configuration except as an engineering change with its own test evidence. If the data show a shortfall, it goes first in the next statement and the next report.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture held to its published terms
other_moves.detail: The terms are those published with the 2035 commitment [P-1233][P-1875]. Risk, investment and revenue are shared, with both partners on one engine. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property. Partner contributions are recognised only as a valuation in the share split, with no licence and no cash payment to the partner. Partner content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, and P&W signs durability only on an engine it has tested. Any departure in the definitive agreement is a significant transaction and goes through Finance to the full Board before signature.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture engine offered, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet
other_moves.detail: The offer is on standard terms, priced for value [PX-0055]. No concession, discount, free upgrade or launch-style term goes to Boeing, Airbus or a fleet customer to win a selection or defend NGSA share. Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto applies, and on the grid an fps code-7 selection is worth −0.03. Any fps-specific rating, installation or derivative change is an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence, not a promise. We give no airframer date [PX-0062].

other_moves.move: Whole-life NPV review and round-2 bridge to the Finance Committee; off-grid rival exposure named, not booked
other_moves.detail:
Mitchill presents the review, as UTC's board reviewed the GTF every year [P-1191].

Whole life:
- ΔPV is −1.65: +0.35 of engine value less $2.00B of R&D, charged undiscounted. That is $0.18 of PV per $1 of R&D.
- It is −1.65 against Do Nothing and against a $2B buyback.
- Capitalise is NOT MET, and no order on the grid closes the 1.65 gap.
- His discounted view, about −0.74, is Finance information only.

Bridge to round 2:
- −0.68 against round 2's hold row in S1, and −3.03 against S4 (+1.38).
- Formation was worth +2.35. CFM's two moves took −3.03. His rough split, which is inference: the ducted engine about −2.3, the Embraer partnership about −0.75.
- Holding GTF2 in 2035 still kept 17.65 against a cancel. From 2045 forward the engine adds +0.94 of PV at 2026.

Exposures named and not booked:
- A CFM Open Fan launch: by rule −35 pp, or −20 pp with lobbying, for CFM. Favourable to us; size not on the brief.
- An fps without us: below S2.
- An fps 7-yr: direction unknown.
- Airbus Delay Tactics: small and covert.
- Rolls-Royce widebody moves: no effect on us.

This is the baseline for the 2050 bridge.

other_moves.move: Incremental time-on-wing work on the Joint Venture engine and the GTF Advantage kit inside the existing durability budget
other_moves.detail: This is the product answer to CFM's ducted engine, not a price answer [P-0768][PX-0093]. It goes ahead on Eddy's four conditions: (a) time on wing ahead of fuel burn [P-1360], with no new programme, no derivative and no board R&D; (b) each change goes in as an engineering change with its own severe-environment test evidence; (c) its parts rank behind AOG spares and shop material; (d) the in-service engineering team that works the shop findings does the work. Mitchill's condition also applies: it is funded inside the existing durability budget, and any money above that comes to his gate first. If it starts pulling engineers or pacing parts from the shops, we drop it. It changes no payoff on the board.

decision.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. The GTF fleet on the A320neo is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. A large fleet is coming through the shops, so the fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms, and we report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We will report its durability as the fleet data show it, by operating environment, hot and sandy included, and claim no more than that. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
decision.rationale:
Decision: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. These are Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and the only values the brief lists. Premium is $0.00B and `overrides` is empty. The round never reaches the Board's review, so this rationale is the record.

1. The bad number first. ΔPV is −1.65 (yield 98.5%): +0.35 of engine value against $2.00B of R&D. Capitalise is NOT MET, a gap of 1.65. No order, premium or concession on this sheet closes it. The grid has one row: −1.65 in S1 and −1.68 in S2.

2. Starting point and vetoes.
- Eddy proposed hold/hold and passes both of his grounds. Mitchill recommends the same and finds no veto on the orders.
- Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto falls on any concession for the fps code or NGSA share (other-move test 1). I framed that move only to reject it. It is not submitted, and the veto is recorded.
- His conditional ground-4 veto on booking upside is not triggered. The final statement books no fps selection, share projection, Open Fan gain, airframer date or durability figure.
- Eddy has no binding veto. I took his statement advice: the Joint Venture engine has no time-on-wing data either way, so the statement no longer implies a shortfall on it and keeps only the known GTF one.

3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036, in service on NGSA since 2037 on code 7. It meets an fps 10-yr EIS of 2055 (S2) with a 19-year margin, and a 7-yr EIS of 2052. No second development is running.
- The binding readiness test passes.
- Eddy's caution is accepted: the 2036 date held because the board sets ready at launch + 6. That is the rule's outcome, not proof that my dates stopped slipping. I keep discounting my own operating dates [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- The in-service evidence is the bad number. After eight years we have no time-on-wing, LLP-life or shop-visit figures in front of the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and we invent none.
- Parts pass Eddy's ground 2. The ranking is AOG spares, then shop material, then kit parts, then OE, with quality gates before each rate step.

4. Optimise inside it. With one legal row there is nothing to choose on the grid, and the tie-breaks all point the same way:
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is answered. We are on NGSA, and the engine can meet any fps EIS. Applying that RTX-wide line to engines is inference.
- A rival's discount, or CFM's new engine, never moves our price [PX-0055].

5. Weights. I take Mitchill's weights, S1 0.75 and S2 0.25, over my framing draft of 0.70/0.30.
- Against an fps launch: Boeing's latest words on the record are 'not launching a new airplane this year', 'the market case for us isn't there yet' and 'a month late rather than a month early', and it has passed two rounds.
- For one: its NB share fell from 45.1% to 33.1% with the MAX at its cap. That is pressure, not a launch.
- My own incrementalism bias leans the same way, so I do not push S2 above his figure.
- Expected PV: −1.6575, rounded to −1.66. It is −1.659 on my draft and −1.665 on equal weights. Worst column: S2, −1.68.

6. Why S2 is −0.03 (Mitchill, inference on the rules). An fps launched now enters service in 2055 against an NB count that ends in 2056. Code 7 splits that slice three ways. Boeing's gain comes off Airbus, where we already sit. A selection is worth nothing to us on the grid, so we pay nothing for it.

7. Bridge to round 2 (Mitchill confirms; the attribution is the Board's inference and his).
- Against round 2's hold row in S1: −0.68. Against S4: −3.03. Formation was worth +2.35, and CFM's ducted engine and the Embraer partnership took −3.03.
- His rough split is about −2.3 for the ducted engine and about −0.75 for Embraer.
- Year profile (nominal): 2037 −0.1; 2038-40 −1.2/−1.1/−0.9 during the A320 wind-down; then +0.1 to +1.4 to 2054, +1.5 in 2055 and +2.0 in 2056.
- Correction to the Board's text: from 2041 the range is +0.1 to +2.0, not +0.3 to +1.5.
- My PV check gives +0.37 (−0.57 before 2045, +0.94 from 2045), against the brief's +0.35.
- Lesson: in round 2 we held CFM at hold, and it cost 3.03. Off-grid rival exposure is now named beside each column and not booked:
  - A CFM Open Fan launch: by rule CFM loses 35 pp, or 20 pp if it lobbies. Favourable to us; not booked.
  - An fps without us: below S2.
  - An fps 7-yr: direction unknown.
  - Airbus Delay Tactics: small and covert.
  - Rolls-Royce widebody moves: no effect on us.

8. Dividend and debt (Mitchill).
- $0 of new R&D. Programme R&D is $2.00B in total, with no fold-in write-off.
- The published terms carry no Joint Venture cash to the partner.
- The dividend is covered and debt is on its pre-ASR path [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. The stretch is unused.
- −1.65 is 1.5% of EV; it is a PV, not a cash call.

9. Veto checks.
- Mitchill's four grounds:
  - Dividend and debt: not reached, because the envelope passes.
  - Unselected engine: not applicable. The engine is selected and in service.
  - Aggressive terms: pass. No concession is offered, and the concession move is vetoed.
  - Booked upside: pass. The booked number is S1 −1.65.
- Eddy's two grounds:
  - Durability by EIS: pass.
  - Parts and capacity: pass. No live escape is in the brief, though the board models no quality.
- No red-line flag is open.

10. Bias check.
- Optimism on dates: discounted, per point 3.
- Architecture loyalty: the Joint Venture engine is our GTF2 architecture, but I claim no durability for it that the fleet data do not show.
- Value capture: the grid backs it here, since a selection is worth −0.03.

11. Red lines in force, none breached:
- durability first;
- fleet first;
- Joint Venture terms (never the gear or core [P-1233]);
- dividend, then debt, then buybacks;
- value, not share;
- proof before commitment [P-1367];
- no airframer dates [PX-0062];
- narrowbody only [PX-0027].
Shared source on code 7 and equal Joint Venture shares are declared as doctrine relief at $0.00B (franchise defence, inference [PX-0058][P-1292]).

12. Disclosure changes, per the Board.
- Dropped: 'planned to be ready in 2036', 'Today Pratt & Whitney commits' and 'Rolls-Royce has not done so'.
- Now stated as facts on the bulletin: ready since 2036, and flown on NGSA since 2037 alongside CFM.
- Durability: we claim only what the fleet data show. We give no share projection and no airframer date, and we repeat that our gear and core stay ours.

13. Look-ahead to 2050.
- I expect `hold` only on the sheet, with no cancel or withdraw right left.
- Any engine item would be ready in 2056 at the earliest, the last year of the NB count. It must clear the grid alone (≥ 0 against hold, worst column no more than $2B below it) and serve a committed airframe on the record. No premium is available against credibility, which is already met. Mitchill expects any such item to fail.
- Set up now: the −1.65 baseline and the exposure list, so the 2050 bridge needs one line per rival move.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighted heavily. I trust Neil's cash numbers over my own operating dates, and he owned his round-2 miss plainly.
- I adopted his weights (S1 0.75, S2 0.25) in place of my 0.70/0.30. Boeing's latest record and its two passed rounds outweigh the share-pressure indicator. The change is 0.0015 of expected PV.
- I adopted his row arithmetic (−1.6575; worst column S2 −1.68) and his envelope check: $0 new R&D, no Joint Venture cash, dividend covered, debt on its pre-ASR path, stretch unused.
- I adopted his whole-life review: −1.65 against Do Nothing and a buyback; about −0.74 discounted, as information only; +0.94 forward from 2045; 17.65 kept against the 2035 cancel.
- I adopted his bridge. Attribution confirmed: formation +2.35, CFM −3.03, split about −2.3 for the ducted engine and −0.75 for Embraer as inference. That includes his correction of the Board's +0.3 to +1.5 range to +0.1 to +2.0, and his PV check (+0.37).
- I adopted his reading of why S2 is −0.03, and his off-grid exposure list beside each column, named and not booked.
- His binding ground-3 veto on any concession is recorded and respected; the move is not submitted. His conditional ground-4 veto is not triggered by the final statement.
- I took his advice that any statement on time on wing rest on Eddy's data.
- I adopted his 2050 hurdle.
memo_weighing.ops:
His proposal is the starting point, taken as proposed: hold/hold.
- Readiness: confirmed and binding on me. The engine is the folded GTF2, ready 2036 and in service 2037, and it meets fps EIS 2052 or 2055. No second development is running.
- His bias caution is accepted. The held 2036 date is the board's launch + 6 rule, not evidence that our dates stopped slipping, so the company's +1.5 to 2 year derivative-entry prior stands.
- His bad number is accepted as given: no time-on-wing, LLP or shop-visit data after eight years, and no 2036 gate data. We report that and invent nothing. His reporting method goes to the committee: by operating environment, hot-and-sandy leaders separate, LLP life by part family, findings by cause.
- His ground-2 pass and pacing-part ranking are adopted, including his correction that 2044-47 is the OE plateau, not a dated shop-visit peak. His load figures are adopted: 730 to 1,024 (+40%), then 928 to 987 a year.
- His four conditions on the incremental durability work are adopted.
- His configuration-control confirmation is adopted, with the change log going to the committee.
- His statement advice is taken: the line implying a known shortfall on the Joint Venture engine is dropped, and the known GTF shortfall is kept.
- I publish no kit-configuration figure, since his last is 60% in June 2023.
- Weight caveat: Eddy's seat rests on one event, June 2023, so his record is Low. His Joint Venture, configuration and in-service views are seat doctrine. On readiness, parts and capacity I defer to him as the rule requires.

decision.expected_scenario: S1, rivals hold (p 0.75). Boeing does not launch an fps this round. Its latest words on the record are 'not launching a new airplane this year', and it has passed two rounds. NGSA stays in service on code 7 with CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce fitted. Our row scores −1.65.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: `GTF2: hold` (gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr hold) scores −1.65 in S1. It is the only row on the grid, so it is also best in S2 (−1.68).
decision.premium_reason: No premium. The only legal row is also the best row, so there is no doctrine-favoured order that trails and no objective order to buy. Credibility is already met: the Joint Venture engine has been on NGSA since 2037. Capitalise cannot be bought on this grid, because the one alternative column is 0.03 worse. Shared source on code 7 and equal Joint Venture shares are declared as doctrine relief at $0.00B. The $1B team cap and the Board's $0.5B per-item cap are unused.
decision.objective_note:
Restore credibility: MET. A new P&W engine, the Joint Venture engine (the folded GTF2), has been in service on NGSA since 2037. On the board it is locked, because NGSA's code cannot change once the airframe is in service. In the fleet it is kept only by time on wing, and we have no in-service figures yet. That is the bad number.

Capitalise on the GTF: NOT MET, at −1.65, a gap of 1.65. No order on the grid closes it, and S2 is 0.03 worse.

PV given up for either objective: $0.00B.
decision.predictions:
Column probabilities (sum 1.00); expected column S1:
- S1 (rivals hold): 0.75
- S2 (Boeing launches fps 10-yr and selects P&W on code 7; it also stands in for any Boeing launch this round): 0.25

These are Mitchill's weights, moved from my framing draft of 0.70/0.30.

Row expected PV:
- `GTF2: hold` = 0.75 × −1.65 + 0.25 × −1.68 = −1.6575, rounded to −1.66.
- It is −1.659 on 0.70/0.30 and −1.665 on equal weights. On any weights it falls between −1.65 and −1.68.
- Worst column: S2, −1.68.
- Item value against hold: 0, by construction.

board_response.recommendation: R3-1. Write the reasons for holding both fields into `rationale`; include the grid row, predictions, expected_pv_b and premium_b = 0; answer each round-2 recommendation.
R3-2. Close the round-2 withdraw-before-formation test as overtaken; keep the definitive agreement exactly as published; any departure comes through Finance to the full Board.

R3-3. Durability proven in service: Eddy reports time on wing, LLP life against plan and shop-visit findings, including hot-and-sandy, bad number first, no invented figures; partner content only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.

R3-4. Fleet first on pacing parts through the 2044-47 peak and the GTF shop-visit tail; supplier quality gates before each rate step; GTF Advantage kit at standard terms, reported as share of fleet in the latest configuration.

final.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The hard part first. The GTF fleet on the A320neo is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. A large fleet is coming through the shops, so the fleet's spare parts and shop material come ahead of new-engine deliveries. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit at standard terms, and we report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

The Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine grew out of our next-generation geared turbofan. It has been ready since 2036 and has flown on the new Airbus single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We will report its durability as the fleet data show it, by operating environment, hot and sandy included, and claim no more than that. If the data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

The competition is strong, and it should be. We answer it with time on wing and with product, not with price. The Joint Venture's terms stand as published: risk, investment and revenue are shared, and our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property.

Our engine is available, as certified, to any new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
final.rationale:
Decision: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. These are Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and the only values the brief lists. Premium is $0.00B and `overrides` is empty. The round never reaches the Board's review, so this rationale is the record.

1. The bad number first. ΔPV is −1.65 (yield 98.5%): +0.35 of engine value against $2.00B of R&D. Capitalise is NOT MET, a gap of 1.65. No order, premium or concession on this sheet closes it. The grid has one row: −1.65 in S1 and −1.68 in S2.

2. Starting point and vetoes.
- Eddy proposed hold/hold and passes both of his grounds. Mitchill recommends the same and finds no veto on the orders.
- Mitchill's binding ground-3 veto falls on any concession for the fps code or NGSA share (other-move test 1). I framed that move only to reject it. It is not submitted, and the veto is recorded.
- His conditional ground-4 veto on booking upside is not triggered. The final statement books no fps selection, share projection, Open Fan gain, airframer date or durability figure.
- Eddy has no binding veto. I took his statement advice: the Joint Venture engine has no time-on-wing data either way, so the statement no longer implies a shortfall on it and keeps only the known GTF one.

3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- The Joint Venture engine is the folded GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036, in service on NGSA since 2037 on code 7. It meets an fps 10-yr EIS of 2055 (S2) with a 19-year margin, and a 7-yr EIS of 2052. No second development is running.
- The binding readiness test passes.
- Eddy's caution is accepted: the 2036 date held because the board sets ready at launch + 6. That is the rule's outcome, not proof that my dates stopped slipping. I keep discounting my own operating dates [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104].
- The in-service evidence is the bad number. After eight years we have no time-on-wing, LLP-life or shop-visit figures in front of the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and we invent none.
- Parts pass Eddy's ground 2. The ranking is AOG spares, then shop material, then kit parts, then OE, with quality gates before each rate step.

4. Optimise inside it. With one legal row there is nothing to choose on the grid, and the tie-breaks all point the same way:
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is answered. We are on NGSA, and the engine can meet any fps EIS. Applying that RTX-wide line to engines is inference.
- A rival's discount, or CFM's new engine, never moves our price [PX-0055].

5. Weights. I take Mitchill's weights, S1 0.75 and S2 0.25, over my framing draft of 0.70/0.30.
- Against an fps launch: Boeing's latest words on the record are 'not launching a new airplane this year', 'the market case for us isn't there yet' and 'a month late rather than a month early', and it has passed two rounds.
- For one: its NB share fell from 45.1% to 33.1% with the MAX at its cap. That is pressure, not a launch.
- My own incrementalism bias leans the same way, so I do not push S2 above his figure.
- Expected PV: −1.6575, rounded to −1.66. It is −1.659 on my draft and −1.665 on equal weights. Worst column: S2, −1.68.

6. Why S2 is −0.03 (Mitchill, inference on the rules). An fps launched now enters service in 2055 against an NB count that ends in 2056. Code 7 splits that slice three ways. Boeing's gain comes off Airbus, where we already sit. A selection is worth nothing to us on the grid, so we pay nothing for it.

7. Bridge to round 2 (Mitchill confirms; the attribution is the Board's inference and his).
- Against round 2's hold row in S1: −0.68. Against S4: −3.03. Formation was worth +2.35, and CFM's ducted engine and the Embraer partnership took −3.03.
- His rough split is about −2.3 for the ducted engine and about −0.75 for Embraer.
- Year profile (nominal): 2037 −0.1; 2038-40 −1.2/−1.1/−0.9 during the A320 wind-down; then +0.1 to +1.4 to 2054, +1.5 in 2055 and +2.0 in 2056.
- Correction to the Board's text: from 2041 the range is +0.1 to +2.0, not +0.3 to +1.5.
- My PV check gives +0.37 (−0.57 before 2045, +0.94 from 2045), against the brief's +0.35.
- Lesson: in round 2 we held CFM at hold, and it cost 3.03. Off-grid rival exposure is now named beside each column and not booked:
  - A CFM Open Fan launch: by rule CFM loses 35 pp, or 20 pp if it lobbies. Favourable to us; not booked.
  - An fps without us: below S2.
  - An fps 7-yr: direction unknown.
  - Airbus Delay Tactics: small and covert.
  - Rolls-Royce widebody moves: no effect on us.

8. Dividend and debt (Mitchill).
- $0 of new R&D. Programme R&D is $2.00B in total, with no fold-in write-off.
- The published terms carry no Joint Venture cash to the partner.
- The dividend is covered and debt is on its pre-ASR path [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. The stretch is unused.
- −1.65 is 1.5% of EV; it is a PV, not a cash call.

9. Veto checks.
- Mitchill's four grounds:
  - Dividend and debt: not reached, because the envelope passes.
  - Unselected engine: not applicable. The engine is selected and in service.
  - Aggressive terms: pass. No concession is offered, and the concession move is vetoed.
  - Booked upside: pass. The booked number is S1 −1.65.
- Eddy's two grounds:
  - Durability by EIS: pass.
  - Parts and capacity: pass. No live escape is in the brief, though the board models no quality.
- No red-line flag is open.

10. Bias check.
- Optimism on dates: discounted, per point 3.

priorities: 1. Product safety in service comes first. Since the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine has been ready since 2036, the narrowbody question is no longer when we launch. On the brief's figures the Joint Venture engine has about 3,091 Rolls-Royce engines delivered by the end of 2044, about 4,044 by the end of 2045, and roughly 950-990 a year after that. Durability, time on wing, life-limited parts and support at that scale are now the absolute priority. Any Rolls-Royce content entering the in-service engine goes in only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never compressed. P&W's published terms say the same [RG-0027, RG-0025, RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283, R-1476].

2. Protect the widebody core without a board-level widebody programme. The $5B strain is now permanent for any widebody item: the Joint Venture is a narrowbody programme on the record, and it cannot be cancelled once ready. Against the hold row, the Trent 1000 upgrade is −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.46 and UltraFan WB is −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02 (S1-S4). Both lose more than their own bill in every column. Hold both, and keep Trent durability work inside the existing budget [R-1574, RX-0246, RG-0068, RX-0123, RX-0214, RG-0019].

3. Profit over share, with no narrowbody premium. Every narrowbody field can only be held this round. S2 (Boeing launches a 10-year fps and selects us on code 5) is −0.04 against S1 on the hold row, so a Boeing selection adds nothing to us on this grid. Chasing it with price, dates or launch-style terms would be buying share for its own sake. Keep standard terms through the Investment Committee [R-1561, R-1582, R-1011, RX-0081, RX-0097, RX-0213].

4. The balance sheet stays untouched, and cash goes back under the capital frame. No new programme spend is needed this round. The Joint Venture share ($4.00B) and the fold write-off ($1.71B) are already booked. We expect no balance-sheet trigger, an unchanged 30-40% payout, and a buyback cadence decided on fit, value and timing [RX-0242, R-0900, RG-0041, RG-0059, RG-0033].

5. Make the Joint Venture work. Alignment is what IAE lacked. P&W's terms are now public: gear and core stay P&W's, contributions are credited as a valuation in the share split, no licence passes, and partner content comes only after entry into service. We need a governed engineering interface, a shared support network and capacity that does not draw on Trent XWB and Trent 7000 [R-0318, R-1010, RX-0072, R-0916, R-0920, RX-0287, RX-0286].

recommendations.text:
Product safety in service. Watson should report the Joint Venture engine's NGSA fleet to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee against a written standard: time on wing in the specification, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts at full life, and aircraft on ground.
- The fleet grows from about 3,091 Rolls-Royce engines at the end of 2044 to about 4,044 at the end of 2045 (brief §1 sums).
- Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never to hold a date. P&W's published Joint Venture terms say the same, and we hold both partners to it.
- If the in-service data tell us something we do not like, we say so first.

Make the Joint Venture work on aligned terms. That is the IAE lesson.
- The 2045 re-test we asked for in round 2 is closed: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and withdrawal is no longer an option.
- What remains is governance. Agree with P&W one engineering interface and one durability standard. Run a joint support network, with our partner shops added to P&W's rather than replacing them. Have a clear process for crediting each side's technology in the share split.
- The equal-share rule now binds. The 2035 grid showed 31.3% for 2050; the brief now shows 26.4%, after CFM's ducted engine and Embraer partnership entered the record (inference). Bring any Joint Venture share or term question to the Board before it is public.

Hold both widebody items. We note what the hold costs, and what it does not.
- The $5B strain is permanent for any widebody item. On this board neither item can stay within its own bill in 2045, nor in 2050 unless that grid shows otherwise.
- The franchise is at 55.2%, 5.2 points above our line, in every column.
- Defend the Trent 1000 position on the 787 through time on wing, inside the existing durability budget (the about £1bn programme). Watch Boeing's 787 work with GE. A rival-engined 787 Re-engine on the record would trigger our franchise test, as a recommendation.
- Bring a widebody item in 2050 only if a Re-engine is then on the record, with the strain in its row and against the $3B cap and the $1B sub-cap for UltraFan WB.

Commercial discipline. Narrowbody is an option, not a need, and it carries no premium.
- S2 is −0.04 against S1: a Boeing fps selection of Rolls-Royce adds nothing on this grid.
- Offer the Joint Venture engine to any new single-aisle on standard terms, through the Investment Committee: no price concessions, no earlier dates, no launch-style terms.
- Our answer to any doubt about readiness is in-service durability data.

Capital and audit. McCabe should confirm that this round needs no new programme spend, that no balance-sheet trigger applies, and that the 30-40% payout and the buyback cadence follow the capital frame. Narrowbody cash from the Joint Venture ramp should be shown in that frame.
- Bring to the Audit Committee an honest Joint Venture lookback: $5.71B of our own narrowbody money against delivered share, and the $4B narrowbody line missed beyond repair.
- The long-term technology position (UltraFan technology and the demonstrator) stays funded inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not by a grid premium.

Capacity and support for the ramp. Rolls-Royce narrowbody engines run at 953 in 2045 and about 930-990 a year to 2060, against 188 widebody engines.
- Bring the supplier plan: castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, and gearbox and shop capacity shared with P&W under the Joint Venture.
- Confirm that Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support stay ring-fenced. Engineering shared with widebody is the constraint our objective names.

- Against hold, the Trent 1000 upgrade is −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.46 and UltraFan WB is −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02.
- Both lose more than their own bill in every column. Widebody holds at 55.2% everywhere.

(3) Joint Venture in-service data below the written standard on time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts or aircraft on ground. I would re-price the aftermarket, the lookback and any provision, safety first, and say so first. (4) Free cash flow well below guidance. I would revisit the pace of distributions, not support or safety spend. (5) Concessions, earlier dates or launch-style terms added as other moves: I would withhold my support. (6) Delivered numbers: actual NGSA pricing and shop-visit data, in place of the board's 1.6x lifecycle multiple, would move the lookback IRR either way.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. This is a delivery round, and the numbers say so plainly.

I confirm Tufan's grid. Hold is +11.03 / +10.99 / +11.03 / +11.28: +11.05 on his weights and the Board's, +11.08 on the Re-engine stress. Against hold, the Trent 1000 upgrade is −6.48 in S1-S3 and −6.46 in S4. UltraFan WB is −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02, or −8.79 expected. Each buys under $1B of engine value for $7B or $9B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain. To stay within its own bill, either would need $5B of engine value; this board gives at most about $1B. I withhold my signature on both. On this arithmetic both are closed for 2050 too, unless that grid shows otherwise.

No new programme spend. No equity, no new borrowing, leverage unchanged. Payout stays at 30-40%, and buybacks are set on fit, value and timing.

The lookback, plainly. We spent $5.71B of our own narrowbody money against a $4B line: missed, and beyond repair. Delivered share is 23.6% in 2045 and 26.4% in 2050, against 28.0% and 31.3% on the 2035 grid. The fold saved $2.29B; on my reading, CFM's moves took back $3.03B of engine value. On Civil margins of 17-25%, the $5.71B earns about 9-12%, below our mid-to-high teens. It adds value, but it does not yet clear the hurdle.

The job now is the quality of cash: time on wing, shop visits, support.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: A narrowbody engine is fitted only if it is ready by the selecting airframe's EIS. The Joint Venture engine is ready at the bulletin's date (2036, the schedule inherited from a folded Solo). Widebody: the Trent 1000 upgrade counts at launch + 3. UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. A late engine fails as advice: it is not fitted and McCabe prices the downside. It is not a veto ground.
tests.numbers:
Narrowbody:
- Joint Venture engine ready 2036, against NGSA EIS 2037 (2030 + 7). One year of margin. Fitted on code 7 (CFM + P&W + RR) and in service since 2037.
- 2036 is the folded GTF2 schedule shown in the bulletin (2030 + 6). UltraFan NB's own date was 2037, and we never stated anything earlier.
- No live airframe is waiting for an engine. NGSA is in service, and Boeing has launched nothing.
- S2: a 10-year fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055 on code 5, and the Joint Venture engine is ready 19 years ahead. A 7-year fps would enter service in 2052, 16 years ahead.

Widebody (for the record; my orders hold both):
- The upgrade, launched 2045, counts from 2048 (2045 + 3) in every column.
- A correction to the Board's reading that it counts from 2050 in S3-S4. The rules count it at launch + 3 with no Re-engine condition, and the grid agrees: the S3 row (−6.48) equals S1, and S4 is −6.46. Counting from 2050 would remove about 2 of its 14 counting years to 2061 in S3 (inference).
- UltraFan WB, launched 2045, is ready in 2051. A 787 or A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 enters service in 2050 (+5), so in S3-S4 UltraFan WB counts from 2051, a year after the Re-engine EIS. In S1-S2 it earns nothing.
- Engine value each buys (its row against hold, plus its bill and the $5B strain): upgrade $0.52B / $0.52B / $0.52B / $0.54B; UltraFan WB $0 / $0 / $0.72B / $0.98B.

tests.name: No early date
tests.numbers:
I checked the CEO's draft statement sentence by sentence. It contains no year at all.
- 'The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA': a fact on the record, with no date.
- 'Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone': no date. This is the right rule.
- 'If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first': keep it.
- 'Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes': conditional, with no date.
- Nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates, and no claim of a share gain.

Option E's public moves (i)-(iii) also carry no dates: the engine in service and paced on durability; on offer on standard terms with no dates; Trent durability inside budget.

Advice, not a condition: add one support line with no date, such as 'Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, is in place and scaling with the fleet.'

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: Before any narrowbody EIS, a support plan through partner shops must be in place, and it must scale with the fleet (inference). Both narrowbody fields are hold-only this round, so no launch, trigger or commit can create a new EIS. One arises only if a new single-aisle selects the Joint Venture engine.
tests.numbers:
NGSA (EIS 2037):
- The plan was carried live before EIS in the 2035 package: Singapore-model partner shops with repair technology, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team.
- That plan was sized on the round-2 brief for about 1,600 engines by 2042 and 4,700 by 2045.

The actual Rolls-Royce fleet (my cumulative sums of brief §1):
- 115 by 2039, 382 by 2040, 1,456 by 2042, 3,091 by 2044 and 4,044 by 2045.
- That is inside the round-2 sizing, with about 650 engines of headroom.

Forward:
- 4,804 more engines in 2046-50 (928-978 a year): about 8,848 by the end of 2050 and 13,652 by 2055.
- The network must roughly double by 2050.
- P&W holds an equal share of the Joint Venture engine, so the Joint Venture fleet on NGSA is larger than ours (inference). Our shops add to P&W's network; they do not replace it.
- The spares and lease pool and the field team scale with deliveries. Spares for aircraft on ground are ranked fleet first.

A new single-aisle: the earliest EIS is 2052 (a 7-year fps launched 2045). The same network is extended before that airframe's EIS.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: Flag the $5B strain, with the years of overlap, whenever a narrowbody project and a widebody project are both on the record. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development. These are seat and company rules, not my words (inference).
tests.numbers:
My recommended orders are all hold: strain $0 in S1-S4.
- The Joint Venture is on the record and has been ready since 2036. It cannot be cancelled, so any widebody item pays a one-off $5B, in 2045 or in 2050. I confirm the strain is permanent.
- Overlap if launched: upgrade development 2045-48, and UltraFan WB 2045-51, each beside a narrowbody line delivering 953-976 engines a year.
- On their letter, neither item breaks my two red lines. No UltraFan is in development: UltraFan NB folded in 2035, and the Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036. No NB Solo is on the record. The numbers decide the case, not the red lines.
- Unpriced load I flag (inference): engineering changes for our content entering the Joint Venture engine use the same engineers as Trent fleet durability. One engineering programme at a time also means rationing those changes.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. The narrowbody ramp is flagged as advice: it needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity.
tests.numbers:
RR engines a year (brief §1), narrowbody + widebody = total:
- 2045: 953 + 188 = 1,141 (5.1 to 1).
- 2050: 978 + 188 = 1,166 (5.2 to 1).
- Narrowbody peak: 987 in 2051. Range 928-987 a year in 2046-60.
- Total output is 3.3-3.9 times my midterm OE ramp of 300-350 a year.
- Shop visits: I use my CMD figure of 1,100-1,200 a year (RX-0279). It is a widebody-era figure, not a board number, and it was never reconciled with Helen's 1,400-1,500 (RX-0223).

Supplier plan (advice):

- Gearbox and shop capacity shared with P&W under the Joint Venture. The gear is P&W's work-share under its published terms.
- Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply, spares and support ring-fenced, with ring-fence status reported to the Committee alongside the fleet report.

The brief reports no constraint.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
On hold, in every column:
- 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 55.2% in 2050.
- A correction to the frame: 2040 was 58.0%, because the GEnx upgrade counts only from 2042 (58/105 = 55.2%).
- Worst year 55.2%, 5.2 points clear.

Other plans:
- With the upgrade: 60.0% in 2050 (63/105).
- With UltraFan WB: 55.2% in 2050 in every column, because it is ready only in 2051.

Threats:
- Boeing's 787 work with GE is unpriced: 'not a 787 Re-engine order'.
- The board's widebody engine shares do not move with the 787/A350 airframe split. In S3-S4 we stay at 55.2%; Airbus's airframe share is 40.2% in S3.
- A hypothetical further 5 points to CFM would leave us at 52.7% (58/110; inference from the renormalisation rule). The line is not threatened anywhere on the board.

Trent 1000 on the 787 (the CEO's ask 7): on this board, time on wing inside the existing durability budget is enough. We keep improving HP turbine blades and extending the life of life-limited parts on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000. The board's upgrade adds 4.8 points of share, not durability, at −6.48.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: UltraFan technology keeps feeding the in-service fleets. Noted qualitatively only; never a grid adjustment.
tests.numbers:
No grid adjustment.
- UltraFan demonstrator and folded UltraFan NB technology keep flowing into the Trent fleet for time on wing, inside a broadly flat R&D envelope.

tests.name: In-service durability and engineering-change rule
tests.threshold: The Joint Venture fleet is reported against a written standard: time on wing in the specification, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts at full life, and aircraft on ground. Rolls-Royce content enters the certified engine only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence, never to hold a date or win a selection. This is my maturity rule (attr.) applied to a formed Joint Venture (inference).
tests.numbers:
In-service record:
- The brief carries deliveries, not fleet data. I have no time-on-wing, shop-visit, life-limited-part or aircraft-on-ground figures, and I invent none.
- The fleet to report: 3,091 RR engines by the end of 2044 and 4,044 by the end of 2045.

Exposure:

If the data are bad, in this order:

- say it publicly, with the fix and no recovery date we cannot hold;
- spares and lease engines go to aircraft on ground first;

The engineering-change rule is confirmed. The CEO's draft and P&W's published terms both state it.

Governance I propose:
- one engineering interface;
- one durability standard and one fleet report;
- one chief engineer per change;
- each change carries its own test plan, certification basis and fleet-introduction gate, reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee;
- introduction in production and at shop visit once tested (inference).

Crediting:
- A joint technical valuation of each change is recorded at its gate and feeds the share split as a valuation only, with no licence and no cash, under P&W's terms.
- The share question is the CEO's, and it goes to the Board before it is public.
- On this board P&W and RR hold equal narrowbody shares whatever is credited, so crediting is unpriced.

vetoes.plan: All four fields at hold, with the CEO's draft public statement and the other moves in option E
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked. No Civil ground is met: nothing compresses maturity, no public text carries a date, and no narrowbody launch, trigger or commit is possible this round.

At the veto check I would invoke the veto if any of these appears:
(a) a public text gives a date for Rolls-Royce content entering the Joint Venture engine, an UltraFan WB date earlier than launch + 6, an upgrade count earlier than launch + 3, or any Joint Venture date other than the bulletin's;
(b) the rationale counts on our content in the certified engine before its own test evidence, or on UltraFan WB earning before 2051 or without a Re-engine in service;
(c) an engineering change, or the offer of the engine to a new single-aisle, is used to hold or win a date (compressed maturity).

If invoked, the team rule makes it binding. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283].

A request, not a veto ground this round: carry the scaled support plan in the package.

Advice only; not a Civil ground and not a red-line breach.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb launch

Advice only; not a Civil ground.

- Against hold: −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02, or −8.79 on the CEO's and the Board's weights.

vetoes.plan: A widebody item in 2050 (the CEO's option D, readiness side only)
vetoes.ground:
Advice.
- A 2050 upgrade would count from 2053, giving 9 years to 2061.
- A 2050 UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056 and needs a Re-engine in service.
- Both windows are shorter than today's, and each item would need about $5B of engine value just to cover the strain. Today's grid shows $0.54B at most for the upgrade and $0.98B for UltraFan WB.
- On dates, I confirm both are closed unless the 2050 grid shows otherwise. The money test is McCabe's.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- **Fleet data below the written standard.** If the first in-service read on time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts or aircraft on ground is below standard, we say so first, in public with P&W. Engineers and spares go to the fleet ahead of any new item, and I would oppose any 2050 widebody item until the fleet recovers.
- **Content rushed into the engine.** Any proposal to put Rolls-Royce content into the certified engine to meet a date, or to win a selection, without its own test evidence: I would invoke the Civil veto for compressed maturity.
- **A date in public.** Any public date for our content entering the engine, any UltraFan WB date earlier than launch + 6, or an upgrade count earlier than launch + 3: I would invoke the veto.
- **A Re-engine on the record by 2050.** A 787 or A350 Re-engine launched, or announced in a public statement, would make me re-test UltraFan WB and the upgrade on the 2050 grid, with the $5B strain in the row. Each needs about $5B of engine value just to cover the strain.
- **A threat to the 50% line.** A brief projecting our widebody share near the line (a further CFM gain takes it to 52.7%), or a rival-engined Re-engine on the record, would trigger the franchise test, with time on wing as the first lever.
- **Support or capacity limits.** A brief reporting a capacity constraint would make the capacity test live. A new single-aisle selecting the Joint Venture engine would need the support network extended before its EIS.
- **Named airline wins.** Wins on the Joint Venture engine would firm up my confidence in the support ramp.
ops.memo:
All four fields at hold. No Civil veto.

The Joint Venture engine was ready in 2036 and entered service on NGSA in 2037, a year of margin, nothing compressed. We have 4,044 Rolls-Royce engines delivered by the end of 2045 and about 8,850 by 2050.

The fleet. The brief gives deliveries, not fleet data, so I bring the Committee a written standard, not invented numbers: time on wing, shop-visit rate, life-limited parts at full life, aircraft on ground. The gear and core are P&W's, and P&W says its GTF fleet is "still not where our customers need it to be". So one durability standard and one voice: if the data are bad, we say so first.

The rule. Our content goes in only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence and one chief engineer per change, never to hold a date or win a campaign.

Support. The plan was sized for 4,700 engines by 2045, so it covers today's fleet. It must roughly double by 2050. Our partner shops add to P&W's network, not replace it.

Capacity. 953 narrowbody engines against 188 widebody in 2045, five to one. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 stay ring-fenced.

Widebody. 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column. With the strain permanent, the upgrade is −6.48 and UltraFan WB −9.00. Time on wing inside the existing budget defends the 787.

We're absolutely focused on keeping our engines flying and earning for as long as possible.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. The Joint Venture engine with Pratt & Whitney is in service on NGSA. Our job now is to deliver what flies: time on wing, support, durability. Support through our partner shops, alongside Pratt & Whitney's network, is in place and scaling with the fleet. Any Rolls-Royce content that enters that engine goes in as an engineering change with its own test evidence. We don't compress it for anyone. If the in-service data tell us something we don't like, we will say so first. The engine is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues inside our existing budget. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board only in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, a delivery round. All four fields at hold. No Board item.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Start from my proposal: all hold. Both memos recommend the same orders.
2. Binding vetoes. McCabe withholds her co-signature on t1000_upgrade launch and on ultrafan_wb launch (binding). Respected: both stay at hold. Watson invokes no Civil veto. He checked the public statement sentence by sentence and it carries no year. I added his support line, which has no date. Overrides are empty.
3. Expected scenario S1. Weights shown (the brief gives none): mine 0.65 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.10; the Board's 0.70 / 0.05 / 0.15 / 0.10; a Re-engine stress 0.40 / 0.10 / 0.30 / 0.20.
4. Grid rows, with and without each item (ΔPV against the status quo):
- 'UltraFan NB: hold': +11.03 / +10.99 / +11.03 / +11.28. Expected +11.05 on mine, +11.05 on the Board's, +11.08 on the stress. Worst column +10.99 (S2). It is the best plan in every column.
- 'hold + T1000 upgrade': +4.55 / +4.51 / +4.55 / +4.82, so −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.48 / −6.46 against hold. Expected −6.48 on all three weight sets. Worst column −6.48, beyond its own −$2B bill. It buys $0.52-0.54B of engine value for $2B of bill plus the permanent $5B strain.
- 'hold + UltraFan WB': +2.03 / +1.99 / +2.75 / +3.26, so −9.00 / −9.00 / −8.28 / −8.02 against hold. Expected −8.79 on mine and the Board's, −8.59 on the stress. Worst column −9.00, beyond its own −$4B bill. It buys $0 / $0 / $0.72B / $0.98B.
- Each item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights.
5. Premium 0. All hold is the best plan. Shortfalls declined: upgrade $6.48B against the $3B cap; UltraFan WB $8.79B (worst $9.00B) against the $1B sub-cap.
6. Red lines checked on the final orders:
- No UltraFan launch without an airframe to fly it: UltraFan WB with no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record would breach it. Watson and McCabe both flagged this. Struck: it is held.
- No early dates: none in public.
- No new narrowbody value: both narrowbody fields hold, the only legal value.
- One big programme at a time: strain stays $0.
- Balance sheet: untouched.
- Commercial discipline: standard terms only.
No unresolved flag.

WHY HOLD, IN MY OWN TERMS
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]. The upgrade is differentiated on 787 time on wing, but fails 'viable business model' on the strain. UltraFan WB fails 'large market' (no Re-engine) and 'viable business model'.
- My instinct on the 787 is 'Why not?' [RX-0117], and I said we could regain share [RX-0101]. But 4.8 points of share for −$6.48B is share bought at a loss, and 'we are not after market share' [R-1582]. Widebody is safe without it: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column.
- No options management [RX-0051]: a widebody item with no Re-engine to fly is not launched as a hedge.
- The Joint Venture is formed and ready. The 2035 re-test is closed by formation, withdrawal is gone, and the money is booked.

CORRECTIONS TAKEN FROM THE MEMOS
- Watson: widebody share was 58.0% in 2040, not 55.2%. The GEnx upgrade counts from 2042.
- Watson: the upgrade would count from 2048 in every column, not from 2050 in S3-S4. The rules and the grid agree.
- McCabe: the right 2035 benchmark for the lookback is S4, P&W commits (+14.06), not S1. Against it the miss is −$3.03B of engine value, with the fold saving $2.29B.

If the data are bad, the order is: operators and Airbus first, with P&W; then in public, with no recovery date we cannot hold; aircraft on ground first for spares; nothing rushed in.

board_response.recommendation: 2. Make the Joint Venture work on aligned terms (the IAE lesson); the round-2 re-test closed; governance, joint support, crediting; Joint Venture share or term questions to the Board first.
board_response.response:
Taken up.
- The round-2 2045 re-test is closed by formation. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, withdrawal is no longer an option, and jv_with_pw is held as approved.
- Governance is a private other move: one engineering interface, one durability standard, one chief engineer per change, a gate per change, and a joint technical valuation feeding the share split as a valuation only (no licence, no cash).
- Our partner shops are added to P&W's network, not replacing it.
- The equal-share rule binds: 26.4% in 2050 against the 2035 grid's 31.3%.
- Any share or term question comes to the Board before it is public.

board_response.recommendation: 3. Hold both widebody items; Trent 1000 defended by time on wing inside the existing budget; watch Boeing's 787 work with GE; bring a widebody item in 2050 only with a Re-engine on the record, strain in the row, against the caps.
board_response.response: Taken up. Both widebody fields are at hold. Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 durability continues inside the about £1bn programme (a public other move). The 787/GE watch is a private other move. One correction, from Watson: the upgrade would count from 2048 in every column, not 2050 in S3-S4; the grid agrees (S3 equals S1). On McCabe's arithmetic both items are closed for 2050 unless that grid shows otherwise (about −6.7 and −8.6 against hold). We will say so to the Board, not in public.

board_response.recommendation: 4. Commercial discipline: narrowbody carries no premium; the Joint Venture engine on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms through the Investment Committee; no concessions, earlier dates or launch-style terms.
board_response.response: Taken up as a public other move and a line in the statement. S2 is −0.04 against S1 on the hold row, so we chase nothing. Standard 'win-win' terms through the Investment Committee. Our answer to any doubt on readiness is in-service data.

board_response.recommendation: 5. Capital and audit: no new spend, no balance-sheet trigger, payout and buybacks under the frame, narrowbody cash shown in it; an honest Joint Venture lookback to the Audit Committee; technology inside a flat R&D envelope.

6. Public statement: in service and paced on durability; no new dates and nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates; no share-gain claim; any widebody line conditional; medium-term guidance through the Board.
board_response.response: Taken up. The statement carries no year. It says nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates or rates and claims no share gain. The widebody line is conditional on a Re-engine on the record, on the Board, and on paying after the cost of running two programmes. Watson checked it with no veto, and his support line (no date) was added. Any medium-term guidance goes through the Board before release.

board_response.recommendation: 7. Capacity and support for the ramp: supplier plan; gearbox and shop capacity shared with P&W; Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ring-fenced.
Round-2 recommendations carried into 2045 (deliver UltraFan NB at maturity; the Joint Venture commit and its 2045 re-test; hold widebody; commercial discipline; public statement; capital; capacity).
board_response.response:
